title: RAG: Unveiling the Power of Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: No substantive research claim is supported by this workshop abstract
rationale: This is a brief workshop/tutorial description (about 1 page) introducing RAG concepts and a hands-on session using Ollama and LangChain, not a research paper. It presents no methodology, no experiments, no evaluation, and no insights on retrieval reliability, evidence handling, robustness, or any other survey-relevant theme. It is purely a descriptive workshop schedule for practitioners and provides no citable scientific contribution for a survey on robust RAG.
caveat: Workshop abstract with no research contribution; citing it would add no value and risk overclaiming.

title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
supports_claims: Modern neural networks are typically miscalibrated, motivating confidence-based control mechanisms (e.g., abstention, adaptive retrieval) in RAG pipelines.
Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and temperature scaling provide a standard foundation for measuring and correcting model confidence used in downstream RAG action-control work.
rationale: This is the canonical calibration paper introducing ECE/MCE diagnostics and temperature scaling, showing that deep networks tend to be overconfident due to capacity, normalization, and reduced regularization. It is not a RAG paper, but it is widely cited as foundational background whenever a robust-RAG survey discusses calibration, uncertainty estimation, or confidence-thresholded abstention/adaptive retrieval. Including it as background (not main_cite) avoids overstating its direct relevance to evidence reliability while still anchoring the calibration lineage used by action-control methods in RAG.
caveat: Predates and does not address retrieval, evidence quality, or knowledge conflict; risk of overclaiming direct RAG relevance if cited beyond foundational calibration framing.
notes: Useful as background reference for calibration/uncertainty section supporting action_control discussions.

title: RAGAs: Automated Evaluation of Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Reference-free metrics such as faithfulness, answer relevance, and context relevance enable automated assessment of RAG pipelines when ground-truth annotations are unavailable.
LLM-based decomposition into atomic statements and verification against retrieved context can diagnose grounding failures and unreliable evidence use in RAG systems.
Dedicated evaluation toolkits (RAGAs) and datasets (WikiEval) provide standardized infrastructure for measuring how robustly RAG systems handle context relevance and faithfulness.
rationale: RAGAs introduces a widely adopted reference-free evaluation framework with three core metrics (faithfulness, answer relevance, context relevance) directly targeting whether RAG outputs are grounded in retrieved evidence and whether retrieved context is focused — both central concerns for robust RAG under unreliable evidence. It also releases the WikiEval dataset and an open-source library integrated with LangChain/LlamaIndex, making it a backbone reference in the RAG evaluation literature. It fits the main evaluation section of the survey as a standard tool, though its reliance on a single proprietary LLM (gpt-3.5-turbo-16k) and small-scale human alignment (50 Wikipedia pages) should be noted as a limitation. Overclaim risk is low if presented as an evaluator with known LLM-judge biases rather than a ground-truth oracle.
caveat: Metrics depend on a closed LLM judge and were validated on a small (50-page) WikiEval set, so reported human-agreement numbers may not transfer to harder evidence-conflict or adversarial settings.
notes: EACL 2024 System Demonstrations; code at github.com/explodinggradients/ragas, dataset at huggingface.co/datasets/explodinggradients/WikiEval.

title: BEIR: A Heterogeneous Benchmark for Zero-shot Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models
supports_claims: BEIR provides a heterogeneous zero-shot retrieval benchmark spanning 18 datasets and 9 tasks, exposing that in-domain retrieval performance does not predict out-of-distribution generalization—a core concern for RAG retrievers facing unreliable or domain-shifted evidence.

Analysis of annotation selection bias (e.g., lexical bias in TREC-COVID) demonstrates that retrieval evaluation itself can be unreliable, motivating careful evaluation protocols for evidence quality in RAG.
BM25 remains a strong zero-shot baseline while dense retrievers can underperform on shifted domains, informing retriever choice and robustness considerations in RAG pipelines.
rationale: BEIR is a foundational NeurIPS 2021 benchmark that systematically evaluates retrieval models' zero-shot generalization across diverse tasks and domains, making it a backbone reference for any survey discussing evaluation of retrieval components in RAG. Its findings on OOD generalization gaps and lexical annotation bias directly support survey claims about unreliable evidence sources and the limits of in-domain retriever evaluation. It is appropriately placed in main:evaluation as a key benchmark citation for the evaluation perspective. Overclaim risk is low if framed as a retriever-evaluation benchmark rather than an end-to-end RAG evaluation.
caveat: BEIR evaluates retrievers in isolation rather than end-to-end RAG with generators, and is English-only with limited long-document and multi-field coverage; survey should not present it as a full RAG benchmark.
notes: Widely cited foundational retrieval evaluation benchmark; code and data publicly available at UKPLab/beir.

title: DRAGIN: Dynamic Retrieval Augmented Generation based on the Real-time Information Needs of Large Language Models
supports_claims: Dynamic/adaptive RAG can decide when to retrieve based on token-level uncertainty, attention importance, and semantic content rather than fixed rules.
Query formulation that leverages self-attention over the full generated context can better capture the model's real-time information needs than using only the last sentence or last few tokens.
Unnecessary retrieval can introduce noisy evidence and harm generation quality, motivating selective/adaptive retrieval triggers.
rationale: DRAGIN is an ACL 2024 long paper that proposes a dynamic RAG framework with two well-defined modules: RIND for retrieval timing (combining entropy, max self-attention, and stopword filtering) and QFS for query formulation from self-attention over the full context. It explicitly frames unnecessary or poorly-timed retrieval as a source of noisy/unreliable evidence, making it a natural citation for the action-control axis of robust RAG (when/what to retrieve, adaptive triggering). It compares against FLARE, IRCoT, IC-RALM, and RETRO baselines on 4 knowledge-intensive datasets with 3 LLMs, providing useful empirical grounding for adaptive-retrieval claims.
caveat: The method requires access to internal self-attention scores, limiting applicability to API-only LLMs; evaluation is limited to knowledge-intensive QA and does not test under adversarial or corrupted-corpus conditions.
notes: Code/data available at https://github.com/oneal2000/DRAGIN; strong fit for an 'adaptive retrieval / when-and-what to retrieve' subsection in the action-control chapter.

title: RAGViz: Diagnose and Visualize Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Attention-based visualization tools can help diagnose whether RAG hallucinations stem from retrieved evidence or parametric memory.
Interactive document toggling enables qualitative analysis of how individual retrieved passages influence generation.
rationale: RAGViz is an EMNLP 2024 system demo that visualizes token- and document-level attention in RAG pipelines and supports add/remove comparisons of context documents to qualitatively differentiate internal vs external hallucinations. This is useful diagnostic/evaluation tooling for robust RAG analysis but does not propose new mechanisms, benchmarks, or robustness defenses, so it fits as an appendix reference under diagnostic/evaluation tooling. Overclaim risk: the tool itself acknowledges that attention is only a heuristic for influence, so it should not be cited as evidence of attribution faithfulness.
caveat: Attention scores are used as a proxy for influence/grounding without validation that high attention implies actual reliance, limiting interpretability claims.
notes: Demo paper; GitHub repo (cxcscmu/RAGViz) is referenced.

title: Improving the Domain Adaptation of Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) Models for Open Domain Question Answering
supports_claims: Joint end-to-end training of retriever and generator in RAG improves domain adaptation performance over keeping the passage encoder frozen.
Auxiliary reconstruction signals can inject domain-specific knowledge into RAG components during training.
rationale: This paper proposes RAG-end2end, extending the original RAG to jointly update the DPR passage encoder, question encoder, and knowledge-base index, plus an auxiliary statement-reconstruction signal, evaluated on COVID-19, News, and Conversation QA. It is a foundational RAG training method paper rather than a robustness-under-unreliable-evidence contribution: it does not study noisy/conflicting/poisoned evidence, abstention, faithfulness, or attack/defense. It is appropriate as background for retriever adaptation lineage in a robust RAG survey but should not be over-claimed as addressing reliability under unreliable evidence.
caveat: Does not address robustness to noisy, adversarial, or conflicting evidence; gains are domain-adaptation accuracy, not reliability metrics.
notes: HuggingFace open-source implementation mentioned; domain-specific datasets released.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
supports_claims: RAG is defined as combining parametric seq2seq generation with non-parametric retrieval over a dense Wikipedia index, providing the canonical formulation for retrieval-augmented generation.
Non-parametric memory in RAG is updatable (index hot-swapping) and reduces hallucinations relative to parametric-only baselines, motivating reliability concerns the survey addresses.
rationale: This is the seminal NeurIPS 2020 paper introducing RAG (RAG-Sequence and RAG-Token) by coupling DPR with BART for knowledge-intensive tasks. Any survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence must cite it as the foundational formulation and as motivation for grounding, factuality, and updateable memory. It also provides early evidence on hallucination reduction and the value of retrieval, which frame later work on evidence reliability. Overclaim risk is low so long as it is cited as foundation rather than as a robustness/security contribution.
caveat: The paper does not directly address unreliable/noisy evidence, attacks, or calibration; cite as foundational rather than as evidence for robustness mechanisms.
notes: Canonical RAG reference; HuggingFace implementation available.

title: RAGLAB: A Modular and Research-Oriented Unified Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Unified RAG frameworks enable fair comparison of algorithms across aligned generators, retrievers, and instructions.
Reproducible toolkits with standardized benchmarks and metrics (e.g., FactScore, ALCE) support systematic RAG evaluation.
rationale: RAGLAB is a modular, research-oriented toolkit that reproduces six RAG algorithms (Naive RAG, RRR, ITER-RETGEN, Self-Ask, Active RAG, Self-RAG) and evaluates them across ten benchmarks with aligned components. It contributes evaluation infrastructure and fair-comparison methodology relevant to a survey's evaluation/tooling section, though it does not directly target unreliable-evidence robustness, noise filtering, or attack/defense. Appendix citation is appropriate as a reference for reproducible RAG evaluation tooling rather than a main mechanistic claim.
caveat: Primarily a systems/demo paper; lacks direct contributions on robustness, evidence reliability, or knowledge conflict handling.
notes: EMNLP 2024 System Demonstrations; GitHub repo available.

title: RAG-Studio: Towards In-Domain Adaptation of Retrieval Augmented Generation Through Self-Alignment
supports_claims: Joint fine-tuning of retriever and generator with self-curated synthetic data can improve domain-specific RAG robustness to noisy or misleading context.
CoT-based classification of retrieved passages as helpful, irrelevant, or misleading provides a useful signal for training models to better handle unreliable evidence.
rationale: RAG-Studio proposes a self-aligned training framework that jointly fine-tunes the retriever and generator using synthetic data, with a CoT rationale that labels passages as helpful, irrelevant, or misleading. This relates to robustness under unreliable evidence because it explicitly trains the LLM to resist misleading retrieved contexts and aligns the retriever with generator preferences. However, the primary framing is in-domain adaptation rather than reliability/robustness per se, so it fits better as appendix support in a broader survey rather than as a main mechanism reference.
caveat: Robustness to misleading context is a byproduct of the domain-adaptation objective; the paper does not systematically evaluate on adversarial or noisy-evidence benchmarks.
notes: Published in Findings of EMNLP 2024; code available on GitHub.

title: LongRAG: A Dual-Perspective Retrieval-Augmented Generation Paradigm for Long-Context Question Answering
supports_claims: Long-context RAG suffers from chunking-induced loss of global structure and low evidence density, motivating extractor-plus-filter pipelines.
CoT-guided filtering combined with mapping chunks back to source paragraphs can reduce noise and improve robustness over Self-RAG and CRAG on multi-hop QA.
rationale: LongRAG proposes a dual-perspective RAG paradigm with an LLM-augmented information extractor and a CoT-guided filter to handle low evidence density and noisy retrievals in long contexts. It directly contributes to robust RAG under unreliable evidence by filtering irrelevant chunks while preserving global context, and compares against Self-RAG/CRAG on multi-hop benchmarks. Placement in main:modality fits because its core insight is scenario-specific (long-context multi-hop QA) while also informing evidence-construction strategies. Overclaim risk is moderate since gains depend on one-time retrieval quality and on fine-tuning data generated by an LLM teacher.
caveat: Authors note dependence on one-time retrieval quality and potential annotation bias from LLM-generated fine-tuning data; gains are reported on three multi-hop datasets only.
notes: EMNLP 2024 main conference; code at https://github.com/QingFei1/LongRAG.

title: PlanRAG: A Plan-then-Retrieval Augmented Generation for Generative Large Language Models as Decision Makers
supports_claims: Plan-then-retrieve with explicit re-planning improves iterative RAG on multi-step decision-making over structured databases.
Adaptive planning reduces missed data analysis and candidate-selection errors compared to standard iterative RAG.
rationale: PlanRAG extends iterative RAG with an explicit planning and re-planning step for decision QA over RDB/GDB, and introduces the DQA benchmark from two strategy games. It is relevant to robust RAG as an action-control lineage paper (adaptive retrieval, re-planning) and as a structured-data RAG scenario, with reported reductions in missed-data and candidate errors versus iterative RAG. It does not directly tackle unreliable or adversarial evidence, so it fits best as an appendix or control-section reference rather than a core robustness citation.
caveat: Focus is decision-making accuracy on clean game-derived databases, not robustness to noisy, conflicting, or poisoned evidence.
notes: Code and benchmark at github.com/myeon9h/PlanRAG.

title: Selective Classification for Deep Neural Networks
supports_claims: Selective prediction with risk-coverage trade-offs provides a foundational mechanism for abstention in deep classifiers, which underpins later abstention/refusal strategies in RAG systems.
Softmax response and MC-dropout serve as early confidence-rate functions that can guarantee a desired risk with high probability via thresholding.
rationale: This is a foundational NeurIPS paper introducing selective classification (reject option) for DNNs with a guaranteed-risk thresholding procedure (SGR) over softmax response or MC-dropout confidence. It is not about RAG, retrieval, or unreliable evidence, but it is a standard upstream reference for abstention/calibration/selective-prediction mechanisms that robust-RAG action-control methods extend. Appropriate as a background citation in the foundations/abstention section rather than a main mechanistic claim about RAG.
caveat: No retrieval, no multimodal/text RAG setting, and no evidence-conflict treatment; overclaiming direct relevance to RAG would be inappropriate.
notes: Classic selective prediction reference; cite alongside El-Yaniv & Wiener (2010) when discussing abstention foundations.

title: RAG-RLRC-LaySum at BioLaySumm: Integrating Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Readability Control for Layman Summarization of Biomedical Texts
supports_claims: RAG with neural reranking can be applied to biomedical lay summarization to improve factuality and readability
Reinforcement learning for readability control can be combined with retrieval augmentation in domain-specific summarization
rationale: This is a workshop shared-task system paper that applies RAG with neural reranking (ColBERT, BGE) plus PPO-based readability control to biomedical lay summarization using Wikipedia as the knowledge source. While it touches on factuality via Summac/AlignScore and uses reranking to improve evidence selection, it does not contribute methodological insight on robustness to unreliable evidence, knowledge conflict, poisoning, or calibration that would support a survey on robust RAG. The contribution is narrowly application-specific (BioLaySumm task, ranked 11th) and is better omitted than included as a boundary citation.
caveat: Risk of overclaiming robustness contributions; the paper acknowledges Wikipedia bias as a limitation but does not address it methodologically.

title: REALM: Retrieval-Augmented Language Model Pre-Training
supports_claims: REALM established end-to-end pre-training of a latent neural retriever jointly with a knowledge-augmented encoder, a foundational lineage for modern RAG systems.
REALM introduced asynchronous MIPS index refresh and salient-span masking as core techniques enabling scalable learned retrieval over millions of documents.
rationale: REALM is a seminal RAG foundation paper that augments masked language model pre-training with a learned dense retriever and a knowledge-augmented encoder, demonstrating gains on Open-QA benchmarks. It does not directly address robustness under unreliable evidence, noisy retrieval, or adversarial conditions, but it defines the retrieve-then-predict generative formulation, MIPS-based scalable retrieval, and the null-document mechanism that later robust-RAG work builds upon. Background/foundation citation is appropriate; it should not be used to support claims about reliability, conflict handling, or abstention.
caveat: Does not address unreliable evidence, attacks, calibration, or abstention; only foundational RAG architecture and training.
notes: Canonical RAG foundation citation; pair with RAG (Lewis 2020) and DPR in foundations section.

title: RetrievalQA: Assessing Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Short-form Open-Domain Question Answering
supports_claims: Adaptive retrieval methods that decide when to invoke retrieval require careful evaluation, and vanilla prompting is insufficient for guiding LLMs to make reliable retrieval decisions.
Benchmarks targeting knowledge absent from LLMs can isolate the evaluation of retrieval necessity decisions in adaptive RAG.
In-context demonstrations with time awareness can improve adaptive retrieval without calibration or additional training.
rationale: This ACL Findings 2024 paper introduces RetrievalQA, a benchmark of 1,271 short-form QA items whose answers are not in LLM parametric knowledge, enabling clean evaluation of adaptive retrieval decisions. It systematically compares calibration-based (e.g., Self-RAG threshold tuning) and model-based (vanilla prompting) ARAG approaches and proposes TA-ARE, a simple ICL-based method. The work is directly relevant to the action-control axis of robust RAG (when to retrieve, abstention, adaptive routing) and also contributes evaluation insight, making main_cite under main:control appropriate.
caveat: Scope is limited to short-form open-domain QA; does not assess long-form generation, retrieval quality, or noisy-context robustness directly.
notes: Useful as both an adaptive-retrieval method reference and a benchmark for ARAG evaluation.

title: LI-RAGE: Late Interaction Retrieval Augmented Generation with Explicit Signals for Open-Domain Table Question Answering
supports_claims: Late interaction retrievers (ColBERT) improve fine-grained question-table matching for open-domain table QA RAG.
Joint retriever-reader training with explicit table-level signals and binary relevance tokens enables filtering of unreliable retrieved tables at inference.
rationale: This ACL 2023 short paper proposes LI-RAGE for open-domain table QA, combining a late-interaction retriever with the RAGE loss and a binary 'yes/no' relevance token prepended to generated answers so the reader can flag whether the retrieved table is reliable. The relevance-token mechanism is directly pertinent to robust RAG under unreliable evidence in the structured-table scenario, and the joint training scheme is a useful design point for the modality chapter. It is a narrow scenario contribution rather than a foundational mechanism, so appendix or modality case_study placement fits best.
caveat: Scope is limited to look-up table QA on two datasets; the reliability signal is binary and tied to a specific seq2seq reader, so generalization claims to broader unreliable-evidence settings should be cautious.
notes: Code at github.com/amazon-science/robust-tableqa; ColBERTv2 base code from stanford-futuredata/ColBERT.

title: Patent Response System Optimised for Faithfulness: Procedural Knowledge Embodiment with Knowledge Graph and Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Domain-specific RAG systems can combine knowledge graphs of precedents with fine-tuned LLMs to improve faithfulness in legal/patent generation.
A six-type unfaithfulness error taxonomy (intrinsic/extrinsic entity and event errors, reasoning coherence, irrelevant evidence) can diagnose RAG output reliability.
Using a consistent LLM across retriever and generator modules may outperform mixed-LLM RAG pipelines in domain settings.
rationale: The paper proposes PRO, a patent response framework combining a domain-tuned LLM (PRLLM), a patent precedent KG (PPNet), and RAG to reduce unfaithfulness in generated responses. It contributes a six-category error taxonomy and human evaluation protocol relevant to faithfulness diagnostics in RAG outputs, and demonstrates KG+RAG integration in a legal/procedural domain. Best placed in an appendix on domain-specific or KG-augmented RAG case studies; the contribution to general robust-RAG methodology is limited since the techniques are tightly coupled to patent procedural knowledge.
caveat: Highly domain-specific (patent law); evaluation is human-based on a private dataset with no public code/data, and faithfulness metrics are partially custom and not directly comparable to general RAG benchmarks.

title: AutoRAG-HP: Automatic Online Hyper-Parameter Tuning for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Online hyper-parameter tuning of RAG components (top-k, compression ratio, embedding) can be cast as a multi-armed bandit problem and addressed with hierarchical UCB methods.
Adaptive selection of RAG configurations can reduce LLM API calls compared to grid search while preserving retrieval recall.
rationale: The paper formulates RAG hyper-parameter tuning as an online multi-armed bandit problem and proposes a two-level Hierarchical MAB (Hier-UCB) to jointly tune top-k, compression ratio, and embedding model. It is primarily an AutoML/optimization contribution rather than a study on robustness to unreliable evidence, knowledge conflict, or attack/defense. It could provide background context for adaptive RAG configuration but does not directly address evidence reliability, faithfulness, or abstention, so background-only placement is appropriate.
caveat: The paper does not address noisy, conflicting, or adversarial evidence; citing it as a robust-RAG mechanism would overclaim, since its 'adaptation' is about hyper-parameters, not evidence quality.
notes: Code link aka.ms/autorag mentioned; GitHub link in extracted signals appears truncated.

title: Reducing hallucination in structured outputs via Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: RAG can reduce hallucination in structured output generation by grounding the LLM in retrieved schema-valid items (steps and table names)
A small fine-tuned retriever paired with a moderately sized LLM can match or exceed a much larger LLM without retrieval, including in out-of-distribution settings
rationale: The paper is an industrial case study showing that RAG over JSON step and table indices reduces hallucinated entities (from up to 21 percent down to under 7.5 percent) in a workflow generation task and improves OOD generalization. It is relevant to a robust-RAG survey as a domain-specific structured-output scenario where evidence quality and retriever recall directly determine output validity. Case-study placement fits because it is application-focused and does not propose new mechanisms for evidence reliability, conflict, or abstention beyond grounding in retrieved candidates. Overclaim risk: the paper measures only one proprietary task and acknowledges residual hallucination even with RAG.
caveat: Proprietary enterprise data and metrics; conclusions on retriever-LLM trade-offs may not generalize beyond JSON workflow generation.
notes: Useful as a structured-output / industrial deployment case study; not a methodological contribution to evidence reliability.

title: BSharedRAG: Backbone Shared Retrieval-Augmented Generation for the E-commerce Domain
supports_claims: Domain-specific RAG benefits from sharing a continually pre-trained backbone between retriever and generator via task-specific LoRA modules.
Constructing higher-quality domain knowledge bases (informative documents and verified QA pairs) reduces noise and conflicting answers compared to user-generated review-based datasets.
rationale: BSharedRAG proposes a backbone-shared RAG architecture with LoRA-based retriever and generator for e-commerce, plus a new WorthBuying dataset with cleaner long-form documents and GPT-4-verified QA pairs. Its relevance to robust RAG under unreliable evidence is mostly indirect: it touches on noisy/conflicting user-generated answers and motivates dataset quality, but does not study poisoning, knowledge conflict, abstention, or noise-robust retrieval mechanisms. Appropriate as an appendix citation under domain-specific/scenario RAG coverage rather than a main mechanism for unreliable-evidence robustness.
caveat: Paper focuses on domain adaptation and joint retriever-generator training rather than explicit robustness to unreliable, conflicting, or adversarial evidence; overclaiming reliability contributions should be avoided.
notes: Artifacts at bsharedrag.github.io; Chinese e-commerce domain only.

title: HyPA-RAG: A Hybrid Parameter Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for AI Legal and Policy Applications
supports_claims: Domain-specific RAG for legal/policy texts benefits from hybrid dense plus sparse plus knowledge-graph retrieval combined with adaptive parameter selection driven by a query complexity classifier.
Custom evaluation frameworks with diverse question types (vague, comparative, rule-conclusion) are needed to diagnose RAG failure modes in high-stakes domains.
rationale: The paper proposes HyPA-RAG, a domain-specific legal/policy RAG system that combines hybrid retrieval (BM25, dense, KG) with a fine-tuned DistilBERT query complexity classifier for adaptive parameter selection, plus a custom evaluation framework with new question types and RAGAS-based metrics. It contributes to robust RAG under unreliable evidence primarily through adaptive retrieval routing and a domain evaluation protocol, but its scope is narrow (single law corpus, LL144) and not a core methodological advance. Appendix placement is appropriate as a domain case for legal RAG with adaptive parameter control and evaluation design.
caveat: Single-corpus study with one human evaluator; classifier trained on synthetic data, limiting generalizability claims.
notes: Useful as a legal-domain RAG case showing query-complexity-driven adaptive retrieval and custom evaluation question types.

title: Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
supports_claims: LLMs exhibit a U-shaped position bias when using retrieved evidence, performing worst when relevant information appears in the middle of long input contexts.

Reader performance saturates well before retriever recall in open-domain QA, indicating that adding more retrieved documents yields diminishing returns and motivates reranking or truncation for robust RAG.
Extended-context models are not necessarily better at using their input context, complicating naive scaling solutions for evidence-rich RAG pipelines.
rationale: This TACL paper provides controlled empirical evidence that LLMs fail to robustly use retrieved evidence depending on its position in the context, with a characteristic U-shaped accuracy curve in multi-document QA and key-value retrieval. It directly informs robust RAG by showing that even when correct evidence is supplied, models may fail to ground on middle-positioned passages, and that more retrieved documents do not guarantee better answers. It is a foundational reference for the model-evidence-use perspective and motivates reranking, context compression, and adaptive retrieval research. Risk of overclaiming is low since findings are specific to evaluated models and prompt formats.
caveat: Findings are tied to specific 2023-era models and prompt formats; later models with improved long-context training may exhibit mitigated but not eliminated positional bias.
notes: Highly influential paper that should anchor any discussion of how LLMs use retrieved evidence under varying context positions and lengths.

title: Model Internals-based Answer Attribution for Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Model internals (gradient-based saliency over context tokens) can produce more faithful answer attributions in RAG than self-citation prompting or external NLI validators.
Self-citation and NLI-based attribution are brittle under instruction-following failures and surface lexical overlap, motivating internals-based faithfulness checks for trustworthy RAG.
rationale: The paper introduces MIRAGE, a two-step internals-based attribution method that detects context-sensitive tokens and traces them to retrieved documents via contrastive feature attribution, then evaluates against self-citation and NLI baselines on XOR-AttriQA and ELI5. It directly addresses faithfulness and grounding of model answers to retrieved evidence—central to robust RAG under unreliable evidence—and documents concrete failure modes of self-citation (missing/wrong citations) and NLI (surface-overlap false positives). It fits the model_evidence_use perspective as a main citation supporting the survey's discussion of attribution/faithfulness mechanisms.
caveat: Evaluated only on 7B open-source LLMs and uses NLI (TRUE) as a proxy reference on ELI5, which the authors acknowledge as a brittleness limitation; generalization to larger models and broader domains is not demonstrated.

title: Two-tiered Encoder-based Hallucination Detection for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in the Wild
supports_claims: Two-tiered encoder classifiers that first filter non-verifiable statements and then check support against retrieved KB can outperform LLM-based hallucination detection in production RAG.
Combining a small amount of in-domain data with public NLI/hallucination datasets meaningfully improves grounding/faithfulness detection in enterprise RAG settings.
Encoder NLI models can be more cost-effective and accurate than decoder LLMs for sentence-level RAG faithfulness checking.
rationale: The paper proposes RAGHalu, a two-tier DeBERTa cross-encoder pipeline (verifiable filter + support classifier) for detecting hallucinations in customer-service RAG outputs, evaluated on four brand datasets plus several public benchmarks. It contributes to the model-evidence-use perspective by providing a faithfulness/grounding detector that distinguishes non-verifiable small talk from unsupported claims and shows the importance of in-domain data and input length on detection quality. As an industry-track applied study with limited methodological novelty for the core unreliable-evidence robustness story, it fits an appendix citation for coverage of hallucination detection and production deployment cost trade-offs.
caveat: Industry-track applied paper focused on customer service domains; results may not generalize and the work does not propose new abstention/control mechanisms inside the RAG generator itself.
notes: Public dataset released at github.com/ilanazim/RAGHalu_public_data; brand data proprietary.

title: Improving language models by retrieving from trillions of tokens
supports_claims: RETRO establishes a foundational retrieval-augmented LM architecture that scales retrieval to trillions of tokens using a frozen BERT retriever and chunked cross-attention.
Quantifying train-test chunk overlap is necessary to disentangle genuine retrieval-driven generalization from leakage-based copying when evaluating RAG systems.
rationale: The paper introduces RETRO, a landmark retrieval-augmented transformer that conditions generation on chunked nearest-neighbor retrieval from a 2T-token database, and reports gains comparable to far larger parametric models. It is a core lineage paper for RAG foundations and includes a leakage-aware evaluation protocol that is mildly relevant to evaluation-design discussions. However, it does not directly address unreliable evidence, noisy retrieval robustness, knowledge conflicts, abstention, or attack/defense, so it belongs in background rather than as a main mechanistic anchor for the survey's central themes.
caveat: RETRO assumes generally helpful retrieval and does not model adversarial, noisy, or conflicting evidence; citing it for robustness claims would overreach.
notes: Foundational RAG architecture paper; leakage analysis section may also support an evaluation-methodology footnote.

title: Detecting Hallucination and Coverage Errors in Retrieval Augmented Generation for Controversial Topics
supports_claims: Hallucination and coverage errors in RAG outputs can be detected using word-overlap, gradient-based salience, and LLM-based classifiers, with classifiers trained on synthetic errors achieving high ROC AUC.
Faithfulness diagnostics for RAG can distinguish content fabricated beyond retrieved evidence from content that drops provided evidence, supporting fine-grained evaluation of grounding.
rationale: The paper formulates neutral-point-of-view response generation as a RAG task and proposes three faithfulness diagnostics (ROUGE, gradient salience, prompt-tuned LLM classifiers) for detecting hallucinations and coverage errors against retrieved arguments. This is directly relevant to robust RAG under unreliable evidence because it operationalizes faithfulness/grounding metrics and distinguishes added vs. omitted content. It fits best as appendix support for the evaluation/faithfulness section since the scenario (controversial topics with curated pro/con arguments) is narrower than the survey's main lineage.
caveat: Scope is narrow (English, ProCon pro/con arguments, single LLM family) and synthetic errors may not reflect realistic noisy retrieval; main contribution is detection rather than mitigation under truly unreliable evidence.
notes: Could alternatively be placed at main:evaluation if the survey emphasizes faithfulness diagnostics.

title: The Good and The Bad: Exploring Privacy Issues in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG)
supports_claims: RAG systems are vulnerable to prompt-based extraction attacks that leak private retrieval database contents.
Integrating retrieval data can paradoxically reduce LLM training-data memorization leakage, while introducing new retrieval-side privacy risks.
Mitigations such as reranking, summarization, and distance thresholds offer partial defenses with privacy-utility tradeoffs.
rationale: The paper empirically demonstrates a novel composite structured prompting attack that extracts private data from RAG retrieval databases on medical dialogue and email datasets, and shows that RAG integration reduces extraction of LLM training data. It is directly relevant to a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence because retrieval data leakage and adversarial prompt extraction represent core security/integrity threats to RAG trustworthiness. Placement in the security section is appropriate as it formalizes a black-box threat model and evaluates several mitigation strategies. Overclaim risk is moderate since findings are tied to specific LLMs and embedding models tested.
caveat: Results are limited to two datasets and a few LLM/embedding combinations; defense evaluations are preliminary and may not generalize.
notes: Strong fit for security/integrity section of a robust RAG survey.

title: Active Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Active retrieval that triggers based on generation-time confidence (low token probability) outperforms fixed-interval or single-shot retrieval in long-form generation.
Forward-looking queries formed from the anticipated next sentence are more effective than past-context queries for adaptive RAG.
Masking low-confidence tokens or generating targeted sub-questions mitigates error propagation when using model-generated content as retrieval queries.
rationale: FLARE is a canonical work on adaptive/active retrieval that decides when and what to retrieve using token-level confidence and forward-looking sentence generation. It directly contributes to the action-control axis of robust RAG (uncertainty-driven retrieval, routing, regeneration) and is consistently cited as a baseline/lineage method in adaptive RAG research. The paper also discusses query-formulation strategies (masking, question generation) that mitigate distractor risk from unreliable LM-generated queries, which ties to evidence reliability. Placement in main:control is appropriate as a backbone reference.
caveat: Calibration assumption (low probability == knowledge gap) may not hold for newer LLMs; the paper does not directly study adversarial or poisoned evidence robustness.

title: Fine-Tuning and Retrieval Augmented Generation for Question Answering Using Affordable Large Language Models
supports_claims: Application-oriented RAG systems for low-resource languages often replace semantic embeddings with keyword/n-gram retrieval due to embedding quality limitations.
LLM-based paragraph filtering can be used to refine retrieved context in multi-step RAG pipelines.
rationale: This is a UNLP 2024 shared-task system description (Sherlock) that combines fine-tuning, DPO, model merging, and a custom RAG pipeline for Ukrainian multiple-choice QA. While it does include LLM-based query decomposition, n-gram keyword retrieval, and LLM-based paragraph filtering, the focus is on winning a competition for a low-resource language rather than on robustness under unreliable evidence, knowledge conflict, calibration, or attack-defense. The contributions are application-specific and provide limited mechanistic insight for a survey on robust RAG.
caveat: Citing this would overclaim its contribution; its RAG design choices are pragmatic for Ukrainian rather than principled robustness mechanisms.
notes: Workshop system paper; ablation only on accuracy, no evaluation of evidence reliability or noise robustness.

title: Exploring Personalized Learning Support through Retrieval Augmented Generation: A Feasibility Study
supports_claims: RAG with query expansion and cross-encoder reranking can be applied to educational task generation across Bloom's taxonomy levels.
Feasibility studies of RAG in personalized e-learning exist but lack empirical validation.
rationale: This is a feasibility-stage application paper that wires together a standard RAG pipeline (Chroma vector store, multilingual MiniLM embeddings, GPT-4 query expansion, cross-encoder reranking) to generate German-language tasks at two Bloom's taxonomy levels. It does not study unreliable evidence, knowledge conflicts, poisoning, calibration, abstention, faithfulness, or any robust-RAG evaluation; the only validation is informal expert feedback. There is no methodological or empirical contribution that a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence would need to cite.
caveat: Application/feasibility prototype only; no robustness, reliability, attribution, or evaluation contribution to the survey topic.

title: ARES: An Automated Evaluation Framework for Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
supports_claims: Automated RAG evaluation frameworks decompose quality into context relevance, answer faithfulness, and answer relevance, using fine-tuned LLM judges over synthetic query-passage-answer triples.
Prediction-powered inference enables tighter confidence intervals on RAG performance using a small human-annotated validation set combined with judge predictions on unlabeled data.
Lightweight fine-tuned judges generalize across in-domain shifts but degrade under drastic shifts (cross-lingual, text-to-code), motivating evaluation-time robustness considerations.
rationale: ARES is a NAACL 2024 paper introducing a widely-adopted automated evaluation framework for RAG systems that explicitly targets context relevance, answer faithfulness, and answer relevance using fine-tuned DeBERTa judges trained on synthetically generated data, with PPI providing statistical confidence intervals. This directly underpins evaluation methodology for robust RAG under unreliable evidence, since faithfulness and context-relevance scoring are central diagnostics for detecting when models misuse noisy or irrelevant retrievals. It belongs in the main evaluation section as a backbone reference alongside RAGAS-style frameworks, with the caveat that it does not specifically address adversarial or poisoned contexts.
caveat: ARES targets general English RAG evaluation and does not specifically test adversarial, poisoned, or knowledge-conflict scenarios that are central to unreliable-evidence robustness; judges also degrade under large domain shifts.
notes: Code/data publicly released on GitHub per abstract; venue is NAACL 2024 main long papers.

title: M-RAG: Reinforcing Large Language Model Performance through Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Multiple Partitions
supports_claims: Partitioning the retrieval database into multiple fine-grained units can reduce noise and focus retrieval on more relevant memories for RAG.
Multi-agent reinforcement learning can jointly optimize partition selection and memory refinement to improve downstream generation quality.
rationale: The paper proposes M-RAG, which partitions the retrieval database and uses two RL agents to select partitions and refine retrieved memories for summarization, translation, and dialogue generation. It is relevant to evidence construction in robust RAG because it addresses noise reduction and memory quality at the retrieval stage, but it does not specifically target adversarial or unreliable evidence (e.g., poisoning, knowledge conflict, misinformation). It is best placed as appendix support for the retrieval-optimization line rather than a main mechanistic citation on unreliable-evidence robustness.
caveat: Improvements are framed in terms of generation metrics on clean benchmarks; the work does not directly evaluate robustness to noisy, conflicting, or adversarial evidence.
notes: No code repository link found; only HuggingFace model and metric URLs were extracted.

title: Controlling Risk of Retrieval-augmented Generation: A Counterfactual Prompting Framework
supports_claims: Counterfactual prompting that perturbs retrieval quality and usage can elicit RAG confidence signals for selective abstention.
Risk-aware metrics (risk, carefulness, alignment, coverage) complement EM/F1 for evaluating RAG abstention under noisy evidence.
RAG models suffer overconfidence on noisy retrieved passages, motivating dedicated risk-control mechanisms beyond LLM-only calibration.
rationale: The paper proposes a counterfactual prompting framework that induces a RAG model to reconsider answers under hypothesized poor retrieval quality or improper usage, then keeps or discards outputs based on answer stability. It introduces an RC-RAG benchmark and four risk-aware metrics (risk, carefulness, alignment, coverage) tailored to abstention under unreliable evidence, evaluating on NQ and TriviaQA with Mistral and ChatGPT. This directly supports the action-control axis of the survey (uncertainty, abstention, refusal in RAG) and offers a concrete method and evaluation protocol for unreliable retrieval contexts.
caveat: Limited to factoid QA in a zero-shot setting; the two latent factors are human-defined and fusion is heuristic, so generalization to multi-hop, long-form, or multimodal RAG is unverified.
notes: Code/benchmark at github.com/ict-bigdatalab/RC-RAG.

title: RAG-HAT: A Hallucination-Aware Tuning Pipeline for LLM in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Hallucination-aware fine-tuning pipelines combining detection and DPO-based rewriting can reduce ungrounded outputs in RAG.
Detection signals with human-readable descriptions can be leveraged to construct preference data for mitigating RAG hallucinations without additional human annotation.
rationale: RAG-HAT proposes a pipeline that trains a hallucination detector on RAGTruth, uses GPT-4 Turbo to rewrite hallucinated outputs, and applies DPO with overly-cautious penalization to fine-tune an LLM for more faithful RAG responses. It contributes to robust RAG by addressing model evidence use (grounding/faithfulness) and shows measurable hallucination reduction with maintained answer quality. Placement in appendix is appropriate because it is one of many hallucination-mitigation fine-tuning approaches, useful for coverage but not a unique mechanistic backbone for the survey.
caveat: Pipeline relies heavily on GPT-4 Turbo for rewriting and label generation, evaluations are restricted to RAGTruth/WebGLM, and the approach does not handle adversarial or noisy retrieval evidence beyond standard hallucination detection.
notes: EMNLP 2024 Industry Track paper; uses RAGTruth dataset; relevant for hallucination mitigation section.

title: Do You Know What You Are Talking About? Characterizing Query-Knowledge Relevance For Reliable Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Goodness-of-fit hypothesis testing over query-document similarity statistics can detect out-of-knowledge queries and trigger abstention in RAG systems.
Synthetic in-knowledge queries generated from corpus chunks can approximate the true in-knowledge distribution for calibrating rejection thresholds.
Embedding models' retrieval accuracy can be misaligned with their ability to detect out-of-knowledge queries, motivating separate diagnostics.
rationale: The paper proposes a statistical framework using GoF tests on retrieval similarity statistics (MSS, KNN, Energy, Fisher/Simes meta-tests) to identify single out-of-knowledge queries online and detect query distribution shifts offline using a two-sample KS test. It evaluates seven test statistics against outlier-detection baselines and LM-based relevance scoring across eight QA datasets and two biomedical corpora, and proposes using synthetic queries as a proxy when in-knowledge queries are unavailable. This is directly aligned with action control / abstention under unreliable retrieval evidence, a core topic for robust RAG, making it suitable as a main citation in the control chapter.
caveat: Experiments are concentrated in biomedical QA with relatively small subsets (300 samples), and synthetic queries may be overly simple compared to real user queries, which limits the generality of the empirical conclusions.
notes: EMNLP 2024 main conference paper; no explicit code/data URLs were extracted from the PDF text.

title: Synchronous Faithfulness Monitoring for Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Synchronous monitoring of decoding dynamics (likelihood, uncertainty, context influence, semantic alignment) enables accurate sentence-level faithfulness detection in long-form RAG.
Faithfulness-oriented decoding via backtracking and beam search improves the faithfulness-informativeness tradeoff over abstention, reranking, and contrastive decoding.
Lightweight aggregators over complementary signals can generalize across tasks and models for trustworthy RAG.
rationale: The paper proposes SYNCHECK, a fine-grained faithfulness monitor that aggregates multiple decoding-time signals to detect unfaithful sentences in RAG outputs, plus FOD which uses these signals to guide beam search for more faithful generation. This directly addresses how models use retrieved evidence and how to detect and correct unreliable/unfaithful generation, which is central to robust RAG under unreliable evidence. It is appropriate for the main faithfulness/grounding section because it both characterizes failure modes and provides an actionable intervention mechanism. The work is venue-published (EMNLP 2024) with released code and benchmarks.
caveat: The method assumes sentence-level granularity and adds inference latency from extra forward passes; gains depend on a trained aggregator and may vary across larger or differently-tuned RALMs.
notes: Bridges model_evidence_use (faithfulness detection) and action_control (decoding-time intervention); could also be cross-referenced in a control/abstention discussion.

title: Exploring Retrieval Augmented Generation For Real-world Claim Verification
supports_claims: RAG can be applied to real-world claim verification by jointly training evidence retrieval and question generation.
Shared task systems on AVeriTeC illustrate fact-checking as a downstream RAG application.
rationale: This is a shared task participation paper that applies a standard RAG framework (dense retrieval plus T5 question generation plus BERT veracity classifier) to the AVeriTeC fact-checking benchmark, ranking 13 of 23. It does not contribute new mechanisms or analyses for robustness under unreliable evidence, attribution, calibration, abstention, or attacks. The connection to robust RAG is only thematic via fact-checking, and the results are modest, so it is not needed as background or case study for the survey. Including it would risk overclaiming relevance to unreliable-evidence robustness.
caveat: Pure system description for a shared task; no robustness, conflict, or unreliable-evidence analysis.

title: $LONG^2RAG$: Evaluating Long-Context \& Long-Form Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Key Point Recall
supports_claims: Evaluation of long-form RAG requires recall-oriented metrics that measure how well generations exploit key information dispersed across multiple retrieved documents.
Performance of LLMs in RAG degrades as retrieved context grows longer, and naive truncation loses essential evidence, motivating robust handling of long, noisy retrieval contexts.
rationale: The paper introduces LONG2RAG, a benchmark of 280 questions with 5 long real-retrieved documents each, and proposes Key Point Recall (KPR) to evaluate how well LLMs exploit key information from retrieved documents in long-form generation. It is directly relevant to the evaluation perspective of robust RAG, particularly the low signal-to-noise and dispersed-information characteristics of real retrieval, and provides empirical evidence on length-induced degradation and truncation losses. Appendix or evaluation-section citation is appropriate because it focuses on evaluation methodology rather than directly on unreliable-evidence robustness mechanisms.
caveat: Focuses on key point recall rather than reliability under adversarial or conflicting evidence; English-only and limited to 280 questions.
notes: Dataset available at https://github.com/QZH-777/longrag

title: Retrieval Augmented Generation with Rich Answer Encoding
supports_claims: Training retrievers to focus on knowledge-relevant rather than only label-relevant passages improves generalization and reduces overfitting in RAG systems.
Rich answer encoding objectives like Dense Knowledge Similarity and Retriever-as-Answer-Classifier can complement standard NLL training for more robust retrieval.
rationale: The paper proposes two auxiliary objectives (RAC and DKS) to train RAG retrievers that prefer knowledge-relevant over label-relevant passages, demonstrating improved retrieval recall and reduced train-dev gap on MSMARCO and KILT-WoW. While it touches on retriever robustness/generalization relevant to RAG evidence quality, it does not directly target unreliable evidence (noise, conflicts, poisoning). It fits as an appendix citation supporting evidence construction and retriever training lineage rather than a main mechanistic claim about robustness under unreliable evidence.
caveat: Paper focuses on training-time retrieval bias rather than on noisy, conflicting, or adversarial evidence; relevance to unreliable-evidence robustness is indirect.

title: OUNLP at SemEval-2024 Task 9: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Solving Brain Teasers with LLMs
supports_claims: Some SemEval system descriptions invoke RAG terminology to denote one-shot in-context learning with retrieved exemplars rather than genuine evidence retrieval.
rationale: This is a SemEval-2024 shared-task system paper that compares GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Gemini, and small open models on brain teasers using prompt engineering, CoT, and a one-shot 'similar/dissimilar riddle' selection via SentenceTransformers cosine similarity over 3,899 scraped riddles. The 'RAG' framing is essentially exemplar retrieval for in-context learning, not retrieval of evidence to ground answers, and the paper offers no analysis of evidence reliability, faithfulness, conflict, calibration, abstention, attacks, or evaluation protocols for robust RAG. It therefore does not support any core claim of a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence and risks overclaim if cited as a RAG method.
caveat: Title uses 'RAG' but methodology is one-shot exemplar prompting; including it could mislead readers about what constitutes RAG in the survey's scope.

title: Retrieval-augmented Generation across Heterogeneous Knowledge
supports_claims: RAG over heterogeneous knowledge sources (text, tables, KGs) can improve coverage when single-source retrieval is insufficient
Naively expanding retrieval corpus to larger but lower-quality sources (e.g., CCNet vs Wikipedia) can hurt QA performance, motivating source-quality-aware retrieval
rationale: This thesis proposal paper surveys and proposes RAG approaches across heterogeneous knowledge (text, tables, KGs), including unified representation, multi-hop retrieval, and structured reasoning. It is relevant for the survey's modality/scenario coverage of cross-source RAG and offers an empirical observation that scaling to a noisier web corpus can degrade performance, which lightly touches on evidence reliability. Because it is a short student research workshop proposal rather than a full methodological contribution, appendix-level citation for coverage is appropriate.
caveat: It is a thesis proposal with preliminary experiments and limited methodological depth; do not overclaim it as a robustness or reliability method.
notes: NAACL 2022 SRW thesis proposal by Wenhao Yu.

title: A Hybrid Retrieval Approach for Advancing Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems
supports_claims: Hybrid retrieval combining dense text embeddings with knowledge graph embeddings can improve retrieval accuracy and ranking for domain-specific RAG
Knowledge-graph-augmented retrieval captures inter-passage global relationships that pure text embeddings miss, supporting better evidence selection
rationale: The paper proposes a hybrid retriever that fuses fine-tuned BGE text embeddings with translational KG embeddings (TransE/RotatE/QuatE) to better capture global passage relations in a health-tech QA use case, and reports modest improvements in HitRate, MRR, and end-to-end answer correctness across several LLM readers. It is relevant to the evidence-construction perspective for KG-augmented retrieval but does not directly study unreliable evidence, noise, conflict, or abstention. Workshop venue with small custom test sets and a single proprietary domain limit its evidential weight, so appendix placement under extended evidence-construction coverage is appropriate.
caveat: Evaluation is on a small proprietary health-tech dataset with LLM-generated synthetic queries; no robustness, noise, or adversarial evidence analysis.
notes: ACL Anthology paper, ICNLSP 2024.

title: Adaptive Contrastive Decoding in Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Handling Noisy Contexts
supports_claims: Adaptive contrastive decoding can dynamically balance parametric and retrieved knowledge based on entropy changes to mitigate the influence of noisy contexts in RAG.
Fixed-weight contrastive decoding methods (CAD, MICD) degrade under noisy retrieval, motivating uncertainty-aware adaptive weighting for robust grounding.
rationale: The paper proposes ACD, a decoding-time method that adjusts the contrastive weight between context-conditioned and parametric logits using entropy reduction as a signal of context informativeness, specifically targeting noisy retrieved contexts in open-domain QA. It directly addresses how models use retrieved evidence under unreliable conditions, making it a strong fit for the model_evidence_use section of a robust RAG survey. The empirical contrast against CAD and MICD across LLaMA/Mistral and three QA datasets provides useful evidence of robustness trade-offs between gold and noisy retrieval. Overclaim risk is limited to short-form QA and base (non-aligned) models, as the authors acknowledge.
caveat: Evaluated only on short-form open-domain QA with base LLMs; behavior under instruction-tuned models and long-form generation is untested.
notes: Could secondarily be tagged action_control due to uncertainty-driven adaptive weighting.

title: ``Knowing When You Don't Know'': A Multilingual Relevance Assessment Dataset for Robust Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Multilingual benchmarks like NoMIRACL evaluate LLM ability to abstain when retrieved passages are non-relevant, exposing high hallucination rates across 18 languages.
Hallucination rate vs error rate on non-relevant and relevant subsets quantifies the tradeoff between over-abstention and over-answering in RAG.
Most open LLMs struggle to balance grounding and refusal under unreliable evidence, while GPT-4 offers the best tradeoff.
rationale: The paper introduces NoMIRACL, a human-annotated multilingual benchmark that explicitly evaluates LLM robustness to unreliable retrieved evidence by splitting queries into relevant and non-relevant subsets and measuring hallucination and error rates. It directly addresses the survey's core theme of knowing when to abstain under unreliable retrieval and provides diagnostic findings across many LLMs and languages. As a venue-published evaluation artifact with public code/data, it is a strong main-text citation for the evaluation perspective and motivates discussion of abstention/refusal action control.
caveat: Limited to Wikipedia corpora and to binary answer-present/not-present classification rather than full answer-quality evaluation; SFT findings are based on small models.
notes: Useful as a cross-cutting evaluation citation that also connects to action_control (abstention) and modality/scenario (multilingual).

title: BERGEN: A Benchmarking Library for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Standardized benchmarking libraries are needed to fairly compare RAG components across retrievers, rerankers, and LLMs.
Surface-matching metrics like EM/F1 poorly capture answer correctness in zero-shot RAG; LLM-based metrics correlate better with GPT-4 judgments.
Retrieval quality (especially with reranking) materially impacts generation quality, while some QA benchmarks do not benefit from retrieval and may be unsuitable for RAG evaluation.
rationale: BERGEN is an open-source library and large-scale empirical study standardizing RAG evaluation across retrievers, rerankers, LLMs, datasets, and metrics with 500+ experiments. It directly contributes evaluation insights relevant to robust RAG: showing surface metrics fail on verbose generations, demonstrating that retrieval quality strongly affects downstream outcomes, and identifying datasets where retrieval hurts or is noisy (e.g., ELI5, WoW). This makes it a strong main-text citation in the evaluation section of a robust-RAG survey.
caveat: Focused mainly on QA and zero-shot evaluation with Wikipedia-based corpora; does not directly address adversarial poisoning or fine-grained unreliable-evidence robustness.

title: Robust Retrieval Augmented Generation for Zero-shot Slot Filling
supports_claims: Hard negative mining and dense negative sampling for DPR improve retrieval quality in RAG pipelines for knowledge-intensive tasks.
Robust training procedures for retrieval-augmented generation can substantially boost end-to-end accuracy on zero-shot slot filling tasks like T-REx and zsRE.
rationale: This EMNLP 2021 paper proposes KGI, a robust RAG variant for zero-shot slot filling that extends DPR with BM25-based and dense-index hard negatives and applies end-to-end RAG fine-tuning, achieving top KILT leaderboard results and demonstrating domain adaptation on a TACRED variant. It is relevant to a robust-RAG survey mainly from the evidence-construction angle (retriever training quality) and as an early example of empirically diagnosing the gap between implicit and explicit knowledge use under retrieval. However, it does not directly address unreliable or adversarial evidence, faithfulness/conflict resolution, calibration, or abstention, so it is best placed as an appendix-level citation for retrieval training lineage rather than a main mechanistic source.
caveat: Robustness here refers to training stability and domain transfer, not to handling noisy, conflicting, or adversarial evidence as targeted by the survey.
notes: ACL Anthology paper; code at github.com/IBM/kgi-slot-filling.

title: Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
supports_claims: Adaptive memory selection via reinforcement learning can outperform fixed Top-K retrieval when evidence requirements vary across queries
Editable memory graphs provide structured evidence management for personalized RAG with dynamic, time-sensitive memories
rationale: The paper proposes EMG-RAG, combining a three-layer editable memory graph with an RL agent that adaptively selects memories instead of fixed Top-K retrieval, addressing data collection, editability, and selectability for personalized smartphone agents. It is relevant to robust RAG mainly through its adaptive (non-fixed-K) selection mechanism and handling of dynamic/outdated evidence via editing operations (insert/delete/replace). It is best placed as an appendix citation under action control or agent/memory scenarios, as the primary focus is personalization rather than unreliable-evidence robustness per se. Overclaim risk: it does not explicitly study adversarial or noisy evidence settings.
caveat: Does not directly target unreliable or adversarial evidence; robustness benefits are inferred from adaptive selection and editability rather than measured under noise/conflict.
notes: EMNLP 2024 main paper; uses Faiss and GPTCache as tooling but no released code for EMG-RAG itself.

title: An Information Bottleneck Perspective for Effective Noise Filtering on Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Information bottleneck objectives can train noise filters that simultaneously maximize useful information and minimize irrelevant retrieved content for RAG.
IB-based filtering can produce empty compressions when retrieved passages are irrelevant, supporting abstention-like behavior under unreliable evidence.
IB provides a unified principle for evaluation metrics, SFT data selection, and RL reward design in noise filtering.
rationale: The paper introduces an information bottleneck framework for filtering noisy retrieved passages in RAG, formalizing the trade-off between conciseness and correctness and explicitly handling the case where retrieval is irrelevant. It evaluates on NQ, TriviaQA, and HotpotQA, achieving very high compression rates while improving answer correctness, which is directly germane to robust RAG under unreliable evidence. It is published at ACL 2024 and contributes both a method and a comprehensive evaluation/training principle for evidence construction. Overclaim risk: the empty-compression behavior depends on filter quality and white-box LLM probability estimates, so abstention is not guaranteed.
caveat: Method depends on white-box LLM probability access for the IB metric and operates only at the extractive filtering level; abstention behavior is heuristic via an additional discard flag.

title: Multi-Level Information Retrieval Augmented Generation for Knowledge-based Visual Question Answering
supports_claims: Multi-level (entity then passage) retrieval with query expansion can mitigate the irrelevant-passage problem in standard single-step RAG for knowledge-intensive multimodal QA.
Joint end-to-end training of retriever and generator using answer-generation feedback helps adapt retrieval to provide more actually-relevant evidence beyond pseudo-relevance heuristics.
rationale: The paper proposes MiRAG, a multi-level RAG that adds cross-modal entity retrieval and query expansion to passage retrieval, jointly trained end-to-end for KB-VQA on ViQuAE. It is directly relevant to the survey's themes of unreliable evidence (noisy pseudo-relevance labels, irrelevant retrieved passages misleading generation) within the multimodal scenario. Appendix placement is appropriate because the contribution is scoped to KB-VQA and entity-aware retrieval rather than offering a general mechanism for robust RAG; it is best cited as a multimodal scenario instance and evidence-construction technique.
caveat: Scope is narrow (ViQuAE KB-VQA with named entities); robustness gains are framed via pseudo-relevance and EM/F1 rather than adversarial or noisy-evidence stress tests.
notes: Code to be released at github.com/OA256864/MiRAG per paper text.

title: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine
supports_claims: Domain-specific RAG benchmarks (e.g., MIRAGE for medicine) systematically vary corpora, retrievers, and LLMs to quantify how each component affects reliability of generated answers.

Medical RAG exhibits log-linear scaling with the number of retrieved snippets and a lost-in-the-middle effect on the position of ground-truth evidence, illustrating how evidence construction quality affects downstream robustness.
Combining multiple corpora and retrievers via reciprocal rank fusion improves robustness across heterogeneous medical QA tasks.
rationale: The paper introduces MIRAGE, a benchmark of 7,663 medical QA questions, and the MedRAG toolkit, systematically evaluating 41 combinations of corpora, retrievers, and LLMs in a high-stakes biomedical setting. It contributes direct evidence on how retrieval components, snippet count, and snippet position affect RAG reliability (including lost-in-the-middle and log-linear scaling), which is highly relevant to a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence. Case-study placement in the modality/scenario section is appropriate because it primarily exemplifies domain-specific RAG evaluation rather than introducing new robustness mechanisms.
caveat: Focuses on multi-choice QA in medicine with vanilla RAG architectures; does not directly study adversarial poisoning, conflicting evidence, or abstention, so claims about general robustness should not be overstated.
notes: Strong artifact availability (MIRAGE and MedRAG GitHub repos) makes it a useful reproducible reference for the medical-scenario subsection.

title: Context Tuning for Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Context augmentation prior to tool retrieval can improve downstream plan generation and reduce hallucinations in RAG pipelines.
Lightweight learning-to-rank approaches (LambdaMART with Reciprocal Rank Fusion) can outperform LLM-based rerankers and fine-tuned semantic search for context retrieval under under-specified queries.
rationale: The paper proposes a context-tuning step that retrieves user/persona context before tool retrieval in a RAG-based planning system, showing improvements in Recall@K, planner accuracy, and reduced hallucination. It is relevant to robust RAG under unreliable evidence because under-specified queries are a form of input unreliability and the paper demonstrates how augmenting and reranking context mitigates downstream errors. However, the scope is narrow (synthetic digital-assistant tool retrieval) and the contribution is more about retrieval/reranking design than core evidence-reliability mechanisms, so appendix placement under extended survey coverage of agent/tool RAG is most appropriate.
caveat: Evaluation relies entirely on GPT-4-generated synthetic personas and queries with a small toolbox; generalization to real-world unreliable evidence settings is not demonstrated.
notes: Workshop paper at UncertaiNLP 2024; useful as a supporting reference for agent/tool RAG and rerank-based context construction.

title: Do Metadata and Appearance of the Retrieved Webpages Affect LLM's Reasoning in Retrieval-Augmented Generation?
supports_claims: Non-textual metadata such as publication date and webpage appearance can causally shift LLM answers under conflicting retrieved evidence, even when source credibility cues are largely ignored.
Conflicting-evidence RAG outcomes depend on signals beyond textual content, motivating robustness analyses that consider metadata manipulation as an adversarial surface.
rationale: The paper conducts a controlled causal study (McNemar tests with swapped metadata) on how publication time, source credibility, and visual webpage formatting affect LLM resolution of conflicting RAG documents, using both ConflictingQA and a new fake-entity variant. This directly supports survey claims about how LLMs use unreliable evidence and how metadata signals can be exploited to bias answers, making it a useful case study for the model-evidence-use and security-adjacent sections. Placement as case_study is appropriate since findings are specific (e.g., model-family sensitivity to CSS formatting and date metadata) rather than a general method. Overclaim risk: limited to 10 LLMs and three metadata types studied independently, not jointly.
caveat: Small sample (355+125 questions), single metadata type per experiment, and no proposed defense or training method; findings are descriptive rather than prescriptive.
notes: ConflictingQA-FAKE dataset and code released; relevant for evidence-conflict and adversarial-metadata discussion.

title: LexDrafter: Terminology Drafting for Legislative Documents Using Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: RAG can be applied to legal terminology drafting in EU legislative documents
Lexical retrieval may reduce noise compared to dense embeddings in domain-specific definition generation
rationale: LexDrafter is a domain-specific application of RAG for drafting Definitions articles in EU legal acts, combining lexical retrieval with Vicuna/LLaMA-2 to generate term definitions. While it briefly mentions noise reduction motivating lexical over dense retrieval, the paper does not address core robust-RAG concerns such as unreliable evidence, knowledge conflicts, faithfulness, attacks, calibration, or abstention. Evaluation is limited to BLEU/BERTScore/BLEURT against ground-truth definitions without diagnostic analysis of evidence quality. The contribution is primarily an applied legal NLP framework rather than a mechanistic or evaluative advance for robust RAG.
caveat: Mention of lexical retrieval reducing noise is anecdotal and not systematically evaluated; citing it as a robust-RAG technique would overclaim.
notes: Domain application paper; could at most appear as a brief boundary example of legal-domain RAG if the survey wants breadth, but not necessary.

title: SEER: Self-Aligned Evidence Extraction for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Model-based evidence extraction with self-aligned learning can outperform heuristic context filtering by jointly optimizing faithfulness, helpfulness, and conciseness of extracted evidence.
Listwise-aware preference optimization (LPO) over model-sampled evidence candidates improves downstream RAG QA accuracy while substantially reducing input context length.
Evidence extractors fine-tuned via self-alignment show improved robustness to irrelevant/noisy retrieved passages compared to base extractors.
rationale: SEER proposes a model-based evidence extractor trained via self-aligned preference optimization with three expert signals (AlignScore-based faithfulness, log-prob-based helpfulness, semantic conciseness), directly tackling unreliable/distracting retrieved content—a central concern for robust RAG. It contrasts with heuristic context filtering (FILCO) and includes a noise-injection robustness study (Section 4.4) showing the aligned extractor degrades less under increasing noise-to-signal ratios. The methodology fits main_cite under evidence construction because it offers both a concrete mechanism (self-alignment with listwise-aware LPO) and empirical evidence on three QA benchmarks. The overclaim risk is modest: experiments are limited to mid-scale generators (Flan-T5-XL, Llama2-7B), single retriever (DPR/Wikipedia), and one HotpotQA case still shows the aligned extractor degrading faster than base under high noise.
caveat: Limited to mid-scale LLMs and a single dense retriever; the expert design still requires domain choices, and robustness gains do not hold uniformly across all noise levels and datasets.
notes: EMNLP 2024 main conference paper; ACL Anthology bibkey likely 2024.emnlp-main.178.

title: TLab at \#SMM4H 2024: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for ADE Extraction and Normalization
supports_claims: RAG with few-shot retrieval can be applied to biomedical entity extraction and normalization from social media without large-scale annotated training data.
rationale: This is a shared-task submission that applies a fairly standard RAG pipeline (SFR-embedding-mistral retrieval + Llama 3 / GPT-4 generation with few-shot prompts) to ADE extraction and MedDRA normalization from tweets. It demonstrates an application of RAG in a biomedical/social-media domain but offers no methodological contribution to robustness under unreliable evidence, noisy retrieval, knowledge conflict, calibration, attribution, or attack/defense. The reported 'robustness' refers only to generalization to unseen MedDRA terms with standard P/R/F1, which is not the survey's focus.
caveat: Including this paper would overclaim, as it does not address evidence reliability, conflict handling, or action control — it is a domain application of off-the-shelf RAG components.

title: Personalised Abusive Language Detection Using LLMs and Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: RAG can inject domain rules into LLMs for personalised classification tasks
Rule-augmented prompting shows partial robustness to contradictory user attribute inputs
rationale: This paper applies a simplified RAG approach (embedding mined rules into prompts) to personalised abusive language detection using GPT-3.5, reporting modest 1.5-4.4% F1 improvements and a small robustness test with contradictory message-attribute pairs. The RAG component is rudimentary (rules hardcoded into prompts rather than retrieved), and the work focuses on a narrow application rather than contributing methodology, mechanisms, or evaluation protocols for robust RAG under unreliable evidence. The contradictory-input experiment is too small and domain-specific to inform survey claims about evidence reliability or action control.
caveat: Application-specific paper with minimal methodological contribution to RAG robustness; the retrieval component is essentially prompt augmentation.
notes: Repository mentioned in paper but URL not extracted in signals.

title: Searching for Best Practices in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Systematic empirical comparison of RAG pipeline modules (query classification, retrieval, reranking, repacking, summarization) yields actionable best practices balancing accuracy and latency.
Fine-tuning generators with a mixture of relevant and randomly-selected documents improves robustness to irrelevant retrieved context while preserving utilization of relevant evidence.
Hybrid sparse-dense retrieval combined with HyDE and reranking (e.g., monoT5) improves evidence quality for downstream generation.
rationale: This EMNLP 2024 paper systematically searches the RAG design space and empirically identifies best practices across the full pipeline, including chunking, hybrid retrieval, HyDE, reranking, repacking, and summarization (Recomp/LongLLMLingua). Crucially for a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence, it studies generator fine-tuning under different context compositions (Dg, Dr, Dgr, Dgg) and finds that mixing relevant and random documents (Mgr) produces a generator that is robust to irrelevant context while still exploiting relevant evidence. The paper also extends to multimodal 'retrieval-as-generation.' It is a strong main-text citation for the evidence-construction pipeline and a useful reference for noise-robust generator training.
caveat: Best-practice recommendations are dataset- and model-specific (Llama2-7B-Chat on selected QA/fact-checking benchmarks); generalization to adversarial poisoning or systematically misleading evidence is not directly evaluated.
notes: Useful as a pipeline-level reference and also for the noise-mixing fine-tuning recipe relevant to robustness.

title: SDG target detection in environmental reports using Retrieval-augmented Generation with LLMs
supports_claims: RAG can be applied to domain-specific tasks like SDG target detection in environmental reports
Lexical vs dense retrieval and prompt design choices affect downstream LLM answer quality in domain RAG
rationale: This is a domain application paper that uses a vanilla RAG pipeline (retrieval + augmentation + generation) for identifying Sustainable Development Goal targets in environmental impact assessment reports.
