It compares lexical vs dense retrieval, prompt variants, and several LLMs, but does not contribute methodological insights on robustness to unreliable evidence, noise, conflicts, attribution, abstention, or attacks. The contribution is mostly a domain test collection and an empirical comparison, which is too narrow for a survey on robust RAG.
caveat: Risk of overclaiming if cited as a robustness or evidence-quality contribution; it is essentially a climate-domain RAG application study.
notes: Test collection and code links provided via bit.ly repository; uses Pyserini for retrieval.

title: LLMs as Collaborator: Demands-Guided Collaborative Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Commonsense Knowledge-Grounded Open-Domain Dialogue Systems
supports_claims: Collaborative LLM-retriever interaction can identify implicit knowledge demands and reduce the cognition gap that produces irrelevant or noisy retrieved facts.
Demand-guided retrieval over commonsense knowledge graphs with explicit fact selection helps filter noisy triples before grounding generation.
rationale: The paper proposes DCRAG, a multi-stage commonsense KG-RAG pipeline for open-domain dialogue that uses LLM-driven Query Production, Topic Planning, Cross Revision, and an explicit Fact Selection step to filter irrelevant retrieved triples. This is relevant to robust RAG insofar as it addresses retrieval noise, information bottlenecks between retriever and LLM, and explicit filtering of unreliable evidence in a graph/KG scenario. However, its core motivation is dialogue quality (engagingness, informativeness) rather than systematic robustness to adversarial or unreliable evidence, so it is best placed in an appendix on KG-grounded dialogue RAG rather than as a main backbone reference.
caveat: Evaluation centers on response quality (GPT-4 and human judgments) rather than controlled noise/poisoning or calibration; robustness claims are indirect.
notes: Code and data released on GitHub; venue is Findings of EMNLP 2024.

title: Optimizing LLM Based Retrieval Augmented Generation Pipelines in the Financial Domain
supports_claims: LLMs exhibit pseudo-helpfulness by generating answers even when gold documents are absent from retrieved context, a key failure mode under unreliable evidence
RAG generation quality degrades with more distractor documents and is sensitive to gold document position in the retrieved list, motivating re-ranking and noise filtering
Instruction following and prompt robustness vary substantially across model families, affecting reliability of RAG deployments in domain-specific settings
rationale: This industry-track paper systematically benchmarks 6 LLMs across 15 retrieval conditions and 9 prompts on two banking datasets, explicitly studying how retrieval failures, distractor noise, and document ordering affect generation quality. It coins and characterizes pseudo-helpfulness (responding when gold is absent), which is directly germane to robust RAG under unreliable evidence. Suitable as a case study in the survey's evidence-use or evaluation section, particularly to illustrate domain-specific failure modes; placement as case_study reflects its empirical-diagnostic value despite non-released datasets.
caveat: Proprietary financial datasets are not released, limiting reproducibility; findings are based on a relatively narrow model set (GPT-3.5/4 and Llama-2 variants) from 2024 and may not generalize.

title: RAG-QA Arena: Evaluating Domain Robustness for Long-form Retrieval Augmented Question Answering
supports_claims: Cross-domain robustness evaluation for RAG-QA requires long-form coherent reference answers that integrate evidence across multiple documents rather than short extractive spans.
LLM-as-judge pairwise evaluation against human-written long-form references can serve as a scalable, reliable benchmark for RAG-QA systems across diverse domains.
rationale: The paper introduces LFRQA, a 26K-query human-annotated long-form RAG-QA dataset across 7 domains, and proposes RAG-QA Arena, an LLM-judge framework that compares model answers to coherent reference answers. It directly addresses evaluation of RAG systems under cross-domain shift, multi-document integration, and conflicting information reconciliation, which are central concerns for robust RAG. Best placed in the evaluation section as a venue-backed long-form, multi-domain RAG benchmark.
caveat: Focuses on answer-quality evaluation and domain robustness rather than directly on adversarial or noisy evidence robustness; LLM-judge bias and cost are acknowledged limitations.
notes: EMNLP 2024 main; useful as a benchmark reference for long-form, multi-domain RAG evaluation.

title: Quebec Automobile Insurance Question-Answering With Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Domain-specific RAG in legal/insurance QA still produces 5-13% answers with false statements, illustrating reliability gaps under specialized evidence
LLMs in RAG pipelines often fail to abstain even when context is insufficient, highlighting the need for action-control mechanisms
rationale: The paper applies an advanced RAG architecture to Quebec automobile insurance QA with GPT-4o, releases two French corpora, and conducts both automatic and human evaluation. Its findings on persistent false statements and the model never abstaining when uncertain provide useful boundary evidence for a robust-RAG survey, particularly regarding domain-specific reliability and abstention failures. However, the contribution is primarily an applied case study rather than a methodological advance in robustness, so appendix placement is appropriate. Overclaim risk: the work does not propose a new robustness mechanism.
caveat: Single-domain French insurance application; no novel robustness method, abstention strategy, or systematic study of unreliable evidence beyond observed hallucination rates.
notes: Released corpora on GitHub; comparisons drawn against InsuranceQA and Open Australian Legal QA.

title: R$^2$AG: Incorporating Retrieval Information into Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Incorporating retriever-side relevance/similarity features into LLM input embeddings via a lightweight bridging module (R2-Former) can help LLMs better discriminate noisy or low-quality retrieved documents.
Bridging the semantic gap between encoder-based retrievers and decoder-only LLMs improves robustness when retrieved evidence contains distractors or irrelevant passages.
rationale: The paper proposes R2AG, which feeds relevance, precedent, and neighbor similarity scores through a small Transformer (R2-Former) and prepends the resulting embeddings to each document as anchors for LLM generation. This is directly relevant to a robust-RAG survey because it explicitly targets the problem of LLMs passively accepting noisy retrieval results and shows gains across multi-hop and long-context QA. It fits an appendix discussion of evidence-use mechanisms that bridge retriever-LLM semantic gaps rather than a main-text backbone, since it is one of several bridging/prompting methods.
caveat: Method depends on encoder-based dense retrievers and small-to-medium open LLMs; robustness is shown on standard QA with provided gold documents, not under adversarial or no-relevant-document settings.
notes: ACL Anthology EMNLP Findings 2024; code at github.com/yefd/RRAG.

title: Retrieval-augmented generation in multilingual settings
supports_claims: Multilingual RAG faces distinct robustness issues including code-switching, language drift to English, and cross-lingual transliteration mismatches that require prompt and metric adjustments.
Off-the-shelf multilingual retrievers handle cross-lingual retrieval reasonably well, but evaluation metrics and prompting strategies need adaptation for unreliable multilingual evidence.
rationale: This workshop paper systematically studies multilingual RAG (mRAG) across 13 languages, identifying robustness failure modes such as wrong reading of provided documents, irrelevant retrieval, code-switching, and language drift. It contributes a character n-gram evaluation metric robust to transliteration variation and analyzes prompting strategies for multilingual evidence use. It fits the survey as a scenario/modality contribution covering multilingual RAG robustness and evaluation, suitable for the modality section or appendix coverage.
caveat: Scope is limited to open-domain QA with Wikipedia datastore and zero-shot prompting; does not propose new defense mechanisms beyond prompt engineering.
notes: Code released as part of the bergen toolkit at github.com/naver/bergen.

title: Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs? A Comprehensive Study and Hybrid Approach
supports_claims: Self-reflection-based routing between RAG and long-context inference can preserve answer quality while substantially reducing cost.
Systematic failure analysis shows RAG struggles with multi-hop, general, complex, and implicit queries, motivating adaptive control under unreliable retrieved evidence.
Long-context LLMs and RAG produce highly overlapping predictions, supporting hybrid routing strategies for robust generation.
rationale: The paper benchmarks RAG against long-context LLMs across LongBench and InfiniteBench, and proposes Self-Route, which uses LLM self-reflection to decide whether retrieved chunks are sufficient to answer or fall back to full long-context inference. This directly contributes to the action-control thread of robust RAG (adaptive retrieval, abstention/routing based on self-assessed sufficiency) and provides a categorized failure analysis of when RAG yields unreliable evidence. Main-text placement under control is appropriate; an overclaim risk is treating Self-Route as a general calibration mechanism when it relies on LLM self-judged answerability, which may itself be miscalibrated.
caveat: Self-Route assumes LLMs are well-calibrated in judging answerability; results depend on prompt design and may not transfer to adversarial or poisoned evidence settings.
notes: EMNLP 2024 Industry Track paper; GitHub link in text refers to needle-in-a-haystack reference, not authors' own released code.

title: Modeling Uncertainty and Using Post-fusion as Fallback Improves Retrieval Augmented Generation with LLMs
supports_claims: Uncertainty signals like 'unknown' responses can trigger adaptive fallback strategies that switch between concatenation and post-fusion for robust RAG.
Multi-round RAG pipelines that condition on model self-awareness of insufficient context outperform single-round concatenation under noisy retrieval.
rationale: The paper identifies two failure modes when LLMs use retrieved passages: 'unknown' outputs even when the gold passage is present, and majority-vote errors in post-fusion. It proposes adaptive multi-round strategies (Concat+PF, PF+Concat) that use the model's uncertainty signal as feedback to switch fusion strategies, which is directly relevant to action-control and uncertainty-aware RAG under unreliable evidence. Placement as appendix_cite reflects its focused workshop scope and standard open-domain QA evaluation, but it provides a concrete instance of uncertainty-driven fallback worth citing.
caveat: Workshop paper limited to three single-hop open-domain QA datasets without testing on multimodal, adversarial, or strongly noisy retrieval settings; the 'unknown' signal is heuristic rather than a calibrated uncertainty measure.

title: RE-RAG: Improving Open-Domain QA Performance and Interpretability with Relevance Estimator in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Relevance estimators with calibrated confidence can detect when retrieved contexts are unhelpful and trigger abstention or parametric-knowledge fallback in RAG.
Reranking with a learned relevance score, trained via weak supervision from QA likelihood, improves both context selection and answer marginalization under noisy retrieval.
rationale: The paper introduces RE-RAG, which augments RAG with a relevance estimator that outputs both relative relevance and per-context confidence, enabling decoding strategies such as answering 'unanswerable' or falling back on LLM parametric knowledge when retrieved evidence is unreliable. This directly contributes to action-control and evidence-construction aspects of robust RAG under unreliable evidence, and is empirically validated on NQ and TriviaQA across small LMs and LLMs. It is appropriate for the main text on control/abstention mechanisms, with a secondary tie to reranking. Overclaim risk is limited to single-hop QA generalization, as the authors themselves note.
caveat: Evaluated only on single-hop open-domain QA (NQ, TriviaQA); generalization to multi-hop, multimodal, or adversarial poisoning settings is untested.
notes: EMNLP 2024 main conference paper; combines reranking and confidence-driven abstention/parametric fallback.

title: Retrieving, Rethinking and Revising: The Chain-of-Verification Can Improve Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Chain-of-verification with scoring, judgment, and query revision can correct unreliable retrieval evidence via adaptive re-retrieval in RAG.
Joint training of QA and verification with CoT rationales improves generation consistency when references are imperfect.
rationale: The paper proposes CoV-RAG, which integrates a verification module that scores references and answers, judges correctness, and revises the query to trigger re-retrieval when evidence appears unreliable. It also unifies QA and verification during training to mitigate internal generation errors even when external references are correct. This directly contributes to robust RAG under unreliable evidence and adaptive action control (re-retrieval/revision), with ablations on revision position and chain structure that are useful comparison points.
caveat: Training data quality depends on GPT-4 synthesis and verification annotations; verification is effectively single-round in deployment and may not generalize beyond open-domain QA.
notes: Findings of EMNLP 2024; relevant for action-control/adaptive retrieval section alongside Self-RAG and rewrite-retrieve-read baselines.

title: SeRTS: Self-Rewarding Tree Search for Biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Tree-search-based adaptive retrieval with self-rewarding feedback can improve evidence quality for domain-specific RAG.
PPO fine-tuning on retrieval trajectories with self-generated feedback can enhance LLM-based query reformulation for biomedical RAG.
rationale: SeRTS proposes Monte Carlo Tree Search combined with a self-rewarding LLM evaluator to iteratively refine queries and assess retrieved documents for biomedical RAG, then uses PPO on the collected trajectories. It contributes an adaptive retrieval/action-control mechanism for handling complex queries and variable document utility in the medical domain, which is relevant to robust RAG under unreliable evidence. Placement in the appendix is appropriate because it is a domain-specific application demonstrating adaptive retrieval rather than a core robustness or evaluation contribution.
caveat: Evaluation is limited to BioASQ with BM25 and small/medium LLMs; the self-reward signal could itself be unreliable, and no direct comparison to noise/adversarial evidence settings is offered.

title: BordIRlines: A Dataset for Evaluating Cross-lingual Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Cross-lingual RAG systems are inconsistent across languages and can be swayed by the language composition of retrieved passages, even when sources are nominally neutral.
Benchmarks targeting contested or perspective-laden queries (e.g., geopolitical disputes) expose evidence-composition biases that standard relevance-only retrieval evaluations miss.
rationale: The paper introduces BordIRlines, a multilingual Wikipedia-sourced dataset of 720 geopolitical-dispute queries across 49 languages, and uses it to probe how varying the language and source mix of retrieved passages alters LLM answers. It contributes an evaluation lens on robustness of RAG under conflicting or perspective-divergent evidence, which is directly relevant to a survey on unreliable evidence. However, the experiments are limited to small-scale case studies rather than systematic dataset-level metrics, so it fits better as appendix-level support for cross-lingual/evidence-composition evaluation coverage than as a main backbone citation.
caveat: Workshop paper with preliminary, case-study-only experiments; no large-scale quantitative robustness metrics yet, and evidence is restricted to neutral-POV Wikipedia, limiting generalization to truly adversarial or unreliable sources.

title: TRACE the Evidence: Constructing Knowledge-Grounded Reasoning Chains for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Constructing knowledge-grounded reasoning chains from retrieved documents can filter noise and improve multi-hop RAG performance under unreliable evidence.
Finer-grained KG triples plus autoregressive chain construction help identify and integrate dispersed supporting evidence more reliably than raw document concatenation.
Adaptive chain termination and grounding selections in KG options mitigate hallucination and irrelevant context propagation in RAG readers.
rationale: TRACE directly targets the unreliable-evidence problem in RAG by converting retrieved documents into a KG and autoregressively building reasoning chains to isolate supporting triples, reducing the impact of irrelevant retrievals on multi-hop QA. Its grounded option-based triple selection and adaptive termination provide a concrete mechanism for evidence construction and noise filtering, with strong gains over vanilla RAG and IRCoT on HotPotQA, 2WikiMultiHopQA, and MuSiQue. This makes it a fitting main-text citation in the evidence-construction section of a robust RAG survey. Overclaim risk is limited because evaluation depends on existing retrieved candidate sets and Wikipedia-style title-anchored KG generation.
caveat: Evidence-quality gains are measured only via downstream QA; KG/chain quality is not directly evaluated, and the method assumes accessible token logits and Wikipedia-style title-text documents.
notes: EMNLP 2024 Findings; code at https://github.com/jyfang6/trace

title: DSLR: Document Refinement with Sentence-Level Re-ranking and Reconstruction to Enhance Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Sentence-level decomposition, relevance-based filtering, and order-preserving reconstruction can refine retrieved passages to reduce distractor noise without additional training.
Unsupervised, off-the-shelf reranker-based refinement generalizes better than dataset-tuned compressors to out-of-domain RAG settings.
rationale: DSLR proposes an unsupervised pipeline that decomposes retrieved passages into sentences, re-ranks them with off-the-shelf rankers above a threshold, and reconstructs them in original order to preserve coherence. This is directly relevant to robust RAG under unreliable evidence as it targets irrelevant/redundant context that distracts the LLM, and provides a comparison with supervised compression (RECOMP) showing better out-of-domain robustness. Appendix citation is appropriate because the contribution is a context-refinement method within the evidence-construction lineage, complementary but not foundational to robustness under adversarial or conflicting evidence.
caveat: Workshop paper with limited adversarial/noise robustness evaluation; gains are modest and threshold T is tuned per model, limiting plug-and-play claims.
notes: ACL 2024 KnowledgeNLP workshop; extracted URLs are third-party libraries, not the paper's own artifact repo.

title: Enhancing Distractor Generation for Multiple-Choice Questions with Retrieval Augmented Pretraining and Knowledge Graph Integration
supports_claims: Knowledge graph triplets can introduce noise that interferes with generation, motivating triplet reranking.
Retrieval can support task-specific pretraining rather than only inference-time augmentation.
rationale: This paper targets distractor generation for multiple-choice questions, proposing a retrieval-augmented pretraining strategy (pseudo-question construction) and a knowledge-graph triplet augmentation pipeline. The retrieval is mostly used to construct pretraining data, and the KG integration is application-focused for MCQ; the only tangential robustness insight is the brief note that KG triplets introduce noise and that the reranker is imperfect. It does not contribute substantive evidence on faithfulness, unreliable-evidence handling, attribution, abstention, or RAG evaluation, so it is not a useful citation for a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence.
caveat: Mentions noisy KG triplets harming generation, but this is anecdotal and not a systematic study of evidence reliability or robustness mechanisms.
notes: Education/MCQ application; RAP is a pretraining augmentation rather than inference-time RAG.

title: Leveraging Passage Retrieval with Generative Models for Open Domain Question Answering
supports_claims: Fusion-in-Decoder established a scalable backbone for processing many retrieved passages jointly, enabling evidence aggregation in RAG-style open-domain QA.
Generative encoder-decoder models can benefit from increasing retrieved-passage counts (5 to 100), motivating later work on noisy/unreliable evidence handling.
rationale: This is the foundational FiD paper that introduced encoding retrieved passages independently and fusing them jointly in the decoder, setting SOTA on NQ/TriviaQA. For a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence, it is relevant as a method-lineage foundation (how RAG models aggregate multi-passage evidence) but does not itself study reliability, noise, conflict, or attack/defense. Background placement is appropriate because it underlies many downstream robustness studies without directly contributing robustness mechanisms or evaluations. Overclaiming risk if cited as evidence of robustness rather than as architectural foundation.
caveat: Paper does not address noise, conflicting evidence, attribution, or abstention; cite only as RAG architectural foundation, not as a robustness contribution.
notes: Classic FiD (Izacard & Grave, EACL 2021); widely cited as the canonical multi-passage generative reader baseline.

title: Towards Cross-Cultural Machine Translation with Retrieval-Augmented Generation from Multilingual Knowledge Graphs
supports_claims: RAG from multilingual knowledge graphs can ground entity-level generation in machine translation and outperform large LLMs on culturally-nuanced entities
Analysis of retriever vs integration shows that even with gold knowledge the generator may fail to use it, indicating a knowledge-integration bottleneck in RAG
rationale: The paper proposes KG-MT, a RAG pipeline that retrieves entities from a multilingual KG and fuses them into an MT encoder-decoder via explicit prompt augmentation and implicit FiD-like embedding fusion, with a new benchmark XC-Translate. It is relevant to the survey as a KG-based RAG scenario and provides a useful diagnostic showing that retriever quality is not the only bottleneck (gold-knowledge upper bound analysis), which speaks to model evidence use under reliable vs unreliable evidence. Best placed in an appendix on KG-RAG and modality/scenario extensions rather than the main robustness narrative, since it does not directly study adversarial or unreliable evidence.
caveat: The paper centers on translation quality and entity coverage, not on robustness to noisy, conflicting, or adversarial evidence; relevance to unreliable-evidence robust RAG is indirect.
notes: Code/data at https://github.com/apple/ml-kg-mt; published at EMNLP 2024.

title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
supports_claims: Dense passage retrieval with dual BERT encoders trained via in-batch negatives substantially outperforms BM25 for open-domain QA retrieval.
Higher retrieval precision typically translates to improved end-to-end QA accuracy, motivating retrieval quality as a key lever in RAG pipelines.
rationale: This paper introduces DPR, a foundational dense dual-encoder retriever trained on question-passage pairs with in-batch negatives plus BM25 hard negatives, establishing strong open-domain QA results. While not addressing unreliable evidence, robustness, or action control directly, DPR is the canonical dense retrieval baseline underlying most modern RAG systems and is appropriate as background for the survey's retrieval foundations. Risk of overclaim: this work does not study evidence reliability, knowledge conflict, or noise robustness.
caveat: DPR is purely a retrieval method; it does not address reliability of evidence, faithfulness, conflict, or adversarial robustness that the survey centers on.

title: Unified Active Retrieval for Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Adaptive/active retrieval that decides when to retrieve is essential for robust RAG, since indiscriminate retrieval can inject irrelevant or harmful evidence.
Multifaceted retrieval-timing criteria (intent, knowledge need, time-sensitivity, self-knowledge) outperform single-criterion approaches like FLARE, Self-RAG, and SKR.
Lightweight plug-and-play classifiers over frozen LLM hidden states enable efficient routing decisions with negligible inference overhead.
rationale: The paper proposes UAR, a unified active-retrieval framework with four orthogonal criteria (intent, knowledge, time-sensitivity, self-awareness) operationalized via plug-and-play classifiers and a UAR-Criteria decision tree, and introduces AR-Bench for evaluating retrieval-timing accuracy. This directly supports the survey's action-control axis on adaptive retrieval and routing under unreliable evidence, showing that retrieval can hurt when knowledge is unneeded or already internalized. It is a strong venue-linked backbone reference for the when-to-retrieve subsection and naturally compares to FLARE/Self-RAG/SKR. Risk: the criteria are heuristic and experiments focus on short-form QA with single-step retrieval, so claims about general robustness should be moderated.
caveat: Limited to single-step retrieval and short-form generation; classifiers may not generalize OOD beyond evaluated scenarios.
notes: Strong fit for action-control/adaptive-retrieval section; AR-Bench may also be cited under evaluation.

title: Unsupervised Information Refinement Training of Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Unsupervised training can teach LLMs to act as information refiners that integrate parametric knowledge with retrieved evidence under varied quality conditions.
Training LLMs to handle three retrieval scenarios (complete, incomplete/incorrect, and irrelevant retrieved texts) improves RAG robustness to noisy and misleading evidence.
Information refinement training enhances zero-shot RAG performance across diverse tasks while preserving generalization.
rationale: The paper proposes INFO-RAG, an unsupervised training method that explicitly addresses three scenarios of retrieved evidence quality including incorrect, incomplete, and irrelevant retrievals, which directly aligns with robust RAG under unreliable evidence. It contributes a model-side mechanism for handling noisy/misleading retrieval and demonstrates robustness gains across 11 datasets. This is a strong main_cite for the model_evidence_use perspective, with clear evaluation of scenario-specific behavior. Code availability supports reproducibility.
caveat: Experiments limited to 7B/13B LLaMA-2 models; the scenario taxonomy is synthetic rather than from real-world noisy retrieval, which may overestimate robustness gains.
notes: ACL 2024 long paper; directly addresses robustness to incorrect/incomplete/irrelevant retrieved evidence.

title: RocketQA: An Optimized Training Approach to Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
supports_claims: Dense passage retrieval with optimized negative sampling (cross-batch, denoised hard negatives, data augmentation) is a foundational retriever for open-domain QA and RAG pipelines.
Denoising hard negatives via a cross-encoder mitigates false negatives in retrieval training, indirectly improving evidence quality.
rationale: RocketQA is a well-known dense passage retrieval training method introducing cross-batch negatives, cross-encoder-denoised hard negatives, and pseudo-label data augmentation, evaluated on MSMARCO and NQ. For a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence, it serves as foundational background on retriever training rather than a direct contribution to reliability, faithfulness, or action control. Its idea of filtering false negatives via a cross-encoder has a mild connection to evidence-quality reasoning but is not a robustness mechanism in the RAG sense. Best placed in appendix/background to acknowledge the dense retrieval lineage without overclaiming relevance to unreliable-evidence robustness.
caveat: Paper is about retriever training quality, not about generator robustness, attribution, or handling noisy/conflicting evidence at inference time.
notes: Canonical dense retrieval baseline; cite as foundation alongside DPR/ANCE if needed.

title: Counterfactuals As a Means for Evaluating Faithfulness of Attribution Methods in Autoregressive Language Models
supports_claims: Counterfactual generation can produce in-distribution inputs for faithfulness evaluation of attribution methods in autoregressive LMs
Token erasure/masking approaches create OOD inputs that confound faithfulness evaluation for instruct-tuned LMs
rationale: This paper proposes a counterfactual-based protocol for evaluating the faithfulness of feature-attribution methods (gradient norm, IG, KernelSHAP, etc.) on autoregressive LMs such as Gemma-2b for sentence classification tasks (SST-2, IMDB, AG-News). It is about interpretability/attribution evaluation in standalone LM classification, with no retrieval, no external evidence, no RAG pipeline, and no notion of unreliable retrieved context. While 'faithfulness' is a shared term, the paper's notion is about token-level input attribution rather than grounding to retrieved evidence, so it does not support claims in a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence.
caveat: Despite shared terminology around faithfulness/attribution, the contribution targets explainability of LM classifiers, not RAG grounding, retrieval robustness, or evidence reliability; citing it would be an overreach.

title: MuRAG: Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generator for Open Question Answering over Images and Text
supports_claims: MuRAG extends RAG to multimodal memory containing images and text, enabling retrieval and reasoning across visual and textual modalities for open QA.
Joint contrastive and generative pre-training over image-text and text-only corpora helps align the retriever with downstream multimodal QA needs.
rationale: MuRAG is a foundational multimodal RAG model that retrieves both images and text from external memory to answer open questions on WebQA and MultimodalQA. It is directly relevant to the multimodal scenario chapter of a robust RAG survey as a representative venue-backed method, though it does not specifically address unreliable evidence, poisoning, or abstention. Its error analysis (counting, recognition, shortcut learning where the model answered correctly despite wrong retrieval) provides useful boundary insight on grounding failures.
caveat: Paper does not target robustness to unreliable evidence, attacks, or calibration; cite primarily for multimodal RAG scenario coverage rather than reliability claims.
notes: EMNLP 2022 anthology paper; shortcut-learning observation in qualitative analysis is useful for faithfulness/grounding discussion.

title: Multi-Hop Paragraph Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
supports_claims: Iterative multi-hop retrieval with query reformulation can improve evidence gathering when a single retrieval step is insufficient.
Sentence-level paragraph representations enable finer-grained retrieval relevance compared to single-vector paragraph encodings.
rationale: MUPPET proposes an iterative multi-hop paragraph retriever that reformulates the question vector using previously retrieved evidence and uses MIPS over precomputed sentence-level encodings, evaluated on SQuAD-Open and HotpotQA. For a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence, it is a foundational retrieval-method reference for multi-hop evidence construction rather than a direct study of robustness, unreliable evidence, or action control. Appendix placement under extended evidence-construction coverage is appropriate; main-text citation would overclaim its relevance to reliability/robustness.
caveat: Paper does not address noise, conflict, poisoning, calibration, or abstention; relevance to 'unreliable evidence' is only indirect through iterative retrieval design.
notes: ACL 2019 venue paper; code at github.com/yairf11/MUPPET.

title: G-Retriever: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Textual Graph Understanding and Question Answering
supports_claims: Graph-based RAG can mitigate hallucination by retrieving structured subgraph evidence directly from textual graphs rather than relying on LLM parametric memory.
Subgraph retrieval can be formulated as a Prize-Collecting Steiner Tree optimization to balance relevance, connectivity, and context-window-aware size control.
RAG over graphs/KGs scales beyond LLM context limits and supports explainability via retrieved subgraph evidence in QA settings.
rationale: G-Retriever introduces a pioneering RAG framework for general textual graphs, formulating subgraph retrieval as a PCST optimization to return connected, query-relevant evidence while fitting LLM context windows. It explicitly demonstrates and quantifies hallucination reduction (e.g., valid node/edge fractions, fully valid graphs) compared to graph prompt tuning, directly speaking to robust RAG under noisy/structured evidence. As a NeurIPS 2024 paper with strong empirical results, code, datasets, and a GraphQA benchmark, it is a backbone reference for the graph/KG modality chapter of a robust RAG survey.
caveat: The retrieval component is static and PCST-based rather than learned; hallucination evaluation on SceneGraphs is based on a relatively small manual sample (100 responses).
notes: Also relevant as evidence_construction (PCST retrieval) and as a hallucination-mitigation case study for graph RAG.

title: Influence Guided Context Selection for Effective Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Context selection based on holistic quality assessment (query-, list-, and generator-aware) can effectively filter noisy/irrelevant retrieved contexts and improve RAG robustness.

Reframing context quality as an inference-time data valuation problem (Contextual Influence value) enables hyperparameter-free selection by retaining only contexts with positive marginal contribution.
A lightweight surrogate model trained with oracle influence supervision plus end-to-end generator feedback can approximate expensive influence computations at inference.
rationale: The paper directly tackles a core robust-RAG problem: noisy/irrelevant retrieved contexts that mislead the generator. It introduces a principled Contextual Influence value that integrates query-, list-, and generator-aware signals, and trains a hierarchical surrogate (CSM) for efficient inference-time filtering, evaluated across 8 knowledge-intensive tasks with two LLM backbones against strong selection/agentic baselines. This is a venue-backbone contribution to the evidence-construction pillar of the survey, justifying main-text discussion in the evidence/context-selection section. Overclaim risk: gains require per-task training of CSM and oracle CI labels, so generalization across tasks/models remains limited (authors acknowledge this).
caveat: CSM currently requires task-specific training with oracle CI value supervision; cross-task generalization and scaling to very large context lists are not fully demonstrated.
notes: NeurIPS 2025 paper with public code (RAG-CSM). Fits naturally alongside RECOMP, Provence, bge-reranker, RankGPT, and information-bottleneck filtering work in an evidence-construction subsection on context selection/compression for robustness against noisy retrieval.

title: Entity-Focused Dense Passage Retrieval for Outside-Knowledge Visual Question Answering
supports_claims: Multimodal RAG for OK-VQA suffers from overly general retrievals and weak supervision signals, motivating entity-focused retrieval that targets critical entities in the visual question.
Constructing stronger positive passages by requiring both correct answer presence and critical-entity grounding can improve retrieval precision and downstream VQA accuracy.
rationale: This paper proposes EnFoRe, an entity-focused dense passage retriever for outside-knowledge VQA that explicitly extracts critical entities from question and image to retrieve more specific, question-relevant Wikipedia passages and improve weak supervision. It is relevant to a robust RAG survey as a multimodal/vision-RAG scenario illustrating how retrieval quality (specificity, sufficiency, relevancy of evidence) can be improved when whole-query encoding is inadequate. Best placed in the multimodal scenario section or appendix as a representative method for evidence construction in VQA RAG, not as a core robustness/unreliable-evidence mechanism.
caveat: Does not directly address adversarial/noisy/unreliable evidence, abstention, or calibration; contribution is primarily retrieval quality in a specific multimodal QA benchmark.
notes: Code at https://github.com/jialinwu17/EnFoRe.git; EMNLP 2022 main conference.

title: Task-Aware Specialization for Efficient and Robust Dense Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
supports_claims: Parameter-efficient dense retrieval architectures with task-aware specialization can improve out-of-domain generalization for ODQA retrieval.
Dense retrievers can underperform BM25 under distribution shift and lexical-overlap settings, motivating architectural improvements to the retriever component of RAG.
rationale: The paper proposes TASER, a Mixture-of-Experts-style bi-encoder for dense passage retrieval that improves parameter efficiency and out-of-domain generalization on EntityQuestions and BEIR. While it touches on retriever robustness to distribution shift, it does not address unreliable or noisy evidence, knowledge conflicts, attribution, or downstream generator behavior central to robust RAG. It is best cited as background on dense retrieval foundations rather than as a main mechanistic contribution to robust RAG under unreliable evidence.
caveat: The 'robustness' here is retriever OOD generalization, not robustness to corrupted, noisy, or adversarial evidence in a RAG pipeline; overclaiming it as a robust-RAG method should be avoided.
notes: Code at github.com/microsoft/taser; published ACL 2023 short paper.

title: RAGTruth: A Hallucination Corpus for Developing Trustworthy Retrieval-Augmented Language Models
supports_claims: RAGTruth provides a large-scale word-level hallucination corpus tailored to RAG, enabling fine-grained evaluation of unsupported or conflicting outputs given retrieved evidence.
Fine-tuning a smaller LLM on RAGTruth yields hallucination detection competitive with GPT-4 prompt-based methods and can be used to suppress hallucinations at inference time.
Benchmarking shows even with retrieved references, leading LLMs produce baseless or conflicting content, motivating dedicated detection and mitigation components in robust RAG pipelines.
rationale: The paper introduces a venue-published, large-scale word-level hallucination corpus specifically for RAG settings across QA, data-to-text, and summarization, with four hallucination types and detailed span annotations. It benchmarks multiple detection methods (prompting, SelfCheckGPT, LMvLM, fine-tuned Llama) and demonstrates that detectors can reduce hallucination rates substantially when used to select among candidate responses. This directly supports an evaluation-focused section on diagnosing unreliable evidence use and model unfaithfulness in RAG, making it a core benchmark resource for the survey.
caveat: Coverage is limited to three English tasks and six specific LLMs from 2023-era models; generalization of the fine-tuned detector to other domains, languages, or newer models is not validated.
notes: Dataset publicly available at https://github.com/ParticleMedia/RAGTruth; useful for both evaluation and faithfulness/grounding discussions.

title: Multi-Task Dense Retrieval via Model Uncertainty Fusion for Open-Domain Question Answering
supports_claims: Ensemble-based mutual information uncertainty can weight multiple domain-specific dense retrievers to handle out-of-distribution queries.
Uncertainty-aware fusion of retrieval experts can outperform joint training and even Bayesian-optimized oracle weights on mixed-domain QA.
rationale: The paper trains independent DPR experts on different QA datasets and uses ensemble mutual information as calibrated weights for fusing their retrieval predictions at test time. This connects loosely to action control via uncertainty-based routing/adaptive retrieval, but it predates LLM-based RAG and addresses neither unreliable evidence robustness, faithfulness, nor generation grounding. It is best cited as background/extended coverage for uncertainty-aware retrieval routing rather than as a core robust-RAG contribution.
caveat: Pre-LLM RAG context focused on dense retrieval expert fusion; does not address evidence reliability, knowledge conflict, or generation-side robustness.
notes: ACL Anthology paper with public code at github.com/alexlimh/DPR_MUF.

title: Unveiling the Magic: Investigating Attention Distillation in Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Attention distillation training for retriever depends heavily on reader quality, with low-quality readers producing ineffective supervision signals.
Token-level analysis can identify when attention-based knowledge distillation between reader and retriever is reliable.
rationale: This short paper investigates attention distillation mechanisms for training retrieval-augmented language models, identifying that reader quality determines supervision signal effectiveness and proposing diagnostic indicators based on answer- and question-related token attention. While it touches on supervision signal reliability during training, it does not address robustness to unreliable retrieved evidence at inference, faithfulness, knowledge conflicts, or evidence-use behavior of the model. Its focus on training-time distillation mechanics makes it tangential to a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence.
caveat: Paper concerns training-time supervision quality, not inference-time robustness to noisy/unreliable retrieved evidence, so citing it could mislead readers about its scope.
notes: NAACL 2024 short paper; no code/data links found in extracted text.

title: Retrieval Augmented Visual Question Answering with Outside Knowledge
supports_claims: Joint training of retriever and generator can mitigate misleading credit assignment that occurs when standard RAG losses reward documents not actually used for answering.
Pseudo-relevance labels are weak signals that may encourage retrieval of misleading documents, motivating combined supervision from model predictions and relevance heuristics.
Diagnostic metrics (HSR/FSR) help disentangle whether retrieved evidence is actually used or whether the model answers from parametric knowledge in multimodal RAG.
rationale: The paper proposes RA-VQA, a joint DPR + generator training scheme for OK-VQA that explicitly addresses how RAG-style losses can up-weight documents that do not actually contribute to answers, and introduces Hit Success Ratio / Free Success Rate diagnostics for retrieval-generation interaction. These insights are useful for a robust RAG survey, particularly for the multimodal scenario and as evidence that pseudo-relevance is unreliable supervision. It is best placed in the multimodal/scenario section or appendix, since the core contribution is OK-VQA-specific rather than a general robustness framework.
caveat: Findings are tied to OK-VQA and a specific image-to-text pipeline; generalization to broader unreliable-evidence settings is not directly demonstrated.
notes: GitHub link is truncated in extracted text but indicates code availability.

title: RAG4GFM: Bridging Knowledge Gaps in Graph Foundation Models through Graph Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Graph RAG can extend retrieval-augmented inference to Graph Foundation Models via multi-level indexing, task-aware retrieval, and feature/topology fusion.
Similarity-based threshold filtering during fusion can suppress low-relevance retrieved subgraphs and noisy edges in graph RAG pipelines.
rationale: The paper proposes RAG4GFM, an end-to-end retrieval-augmented framework tailored to Graph Foundation Models, with hierarchical HNSW-based graph indexing, task-aware retrieval, and attention/topology fusion. While its main goals are knowledge updating efficiency and reducing GFM hallucinations rather than robustness under unreliable evidence, its similarity thresholds for filtering low-relevance retrieved subgraphs and noisy edges, plus its graph-scenario RAG positioning, make it useful as appendix-level coverage for the graph/KG modality in a robust RAG survey. It does not provide direct adversarial, poisoning, or knowledge-conflict analysis, so main-text placement is not warranted.
caveat: Focuses on GFM knowledge updating and hallucination reduction rather than systematic robustness to adversarial or noisy retrieved evidence; no explicit attack/defense or unreliable-evidence benchmarks.
notes: Useful as a graph-RAG scenario citation; relevance to unreliable-evidence robustness is indirect via threshold-based filtering.

title: Retrieval Augmented Generation of Subjective Explanations for Socioeconomic Scenarios
supports_claims: RAG can be augmented with domain-specific filters (causality, subjectivity) to retrieve contextually relevant evidence for socioeconomic explanation generation.
rationale: This workshop paper applies RAG to generate subjective explanations for socioeconomic mining scenarios in Ghana, using causality and subjectivity classifiers to filter retrieved sentences. While it does incorporate evidence filtering, its focus is on capturing local population beliefs rather than robustness, reliability, knowledge conflict, or unreliable evidence handling. The contribution is domain-specific (computational social science) and does not provide mechanistic insight into robust RAG under unreliable evidence.
caveat: Sentence-level filtering by subjectivity/causality is tangential to evidence reliability; the paper does not address noise, poisoning, conflict, or attribution faithfulness in any depth.

title: ReMindRAG: Low-Cost LLM-Guided Knowledge Graph Traversal for Efficient RAG
supports_claims: KG-RAG systems use LLM-guided graph traversal with memory replay to balance effectiveness and cost efficiency for multi-hop and long-dependency queries.
Self-correction via path enhancement/penalization in KG edges enables iterative refinement of retrieval over repeated queries.
rationale: ReMindRAG proposes an LLM-guided KG traversal with node exploration/exploitation and a train-free memory replay mechanism that memorizes traversal experience in edge embeddings, evaluated on LooGLE and HotpotQA. It is relevant to a robust-RAG survey as a graph/KG-RAG modality contribution and demonstrates self-correction of erroneous retrieval paths, which connects to evidence construction quality. However, the paper centers on effectiveness/efficiency rather than unreliable evidence per se, making appendix or modality-section citation more appropriate than main mechanistic claim support.
caveat: Primary framing is cost-efficiency of KG-RAG, not robustness to unreliable or adversarial evidence; self-correction is a side benefit rather than a central claim.
notes: NeurIPS 2025 paper with public GitHub code; useful as KG-RAG scenario reference.

title: Measuring and Enhancing Trustworthiness of LLMs in RAG through Grounded Attributions and Learning to Refuse
supports_claims: Alignment via DPO with paired positive/negative responses can substantially improve LLMs' ability to refuse unanswerable RAG queries and ground answers in retrieved documents.
Holistic trustworthiness metrics combining grounded refusals, calibrated answer correctness, and citation precision/recall expose how parametric-knowledge reliance inflates standard RAG scores.
Disentangling retriever quality from LLM groundedness is necessary to measure robust behavior under insufficient or irrelevant evidence.
rationale: The paper introduces TRUST-SCORE (a metric jointly capturing grounded refusal, answer-calibrated correctness, and citation groundedness) and TRUST-ALIGN (a DPO-based alignment recipe with a 19K preference dataset targeting five hallucination types including over-responsiveness and excessive refusal). It directly addresses robust RAG under unreliable evidence by penalizing parametric-knowledge leakage and training models to refuse when documents are insufficient. Placement in the action_control/refusal section is appropriate, with secondary relevance to evaluation and model_evidence_use. Overclaim risk is modest: improvements are mostly on three QA datasets and depend on the TRUE NLI labeler for answerability.
caveat: Evaluation centers on ASQA/QAMPARI/ELI5/ExpertQA and relies on a TRUE-based NLI judge for answerability, which may not generalize to multimodal, agentic, or adversarial unreliable-evidence settings.
notes: Code released at github.com/declare-lab/trust-align; strong candidate as a backbone reference for refusal/abstention and trustworthiness evaluation in RAG.

title: GFM-RAG: Graph Foundation Model for Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Graph foundation models can serve as transferable retrievers for GraphRAG and address noise/incompleteness in KG-indexed evidence via query-dependent GNN message passing.
Pre-trained GNN-based retrievers can perform multi-hop retrieval in a single step, improving efficiency over iterative LLM-based multi-step RAG pipelines.
rationale: GFM-RAG proposes a query-dependent GNN pre-trained on 60 KGs to retrieve documents from a KG-index, explicitly motivated by the noise and incompleteness of constructed graphs that hurt prior GraphRAG methods like HippoRAG. For a robust-RAG survey, it is a representative graph/KG-scenario backbone that addresses one form of unreliable evidence (noisy/incomplete graph indexes) and improves multi-hop retrieval quality, making it suitable as appendix or modality-section support. It does not directly study adversarial/poisoned evidence, faithfulness, calibration, or abstention, so it should not be promoted as a core robustness contribution.
caveat: Improvements target noisy/incomplete graph structure and multi-hop coverage rather than unreliable-evidence robustness in the security, conflict, or calibration sense; overclaiming its relevance to adversarial robustness should be avoided.
notes: Project page https://rmanluo.github.io/gfm-rag; NeurIPS 2025.

title: VRAG-RL: Empower Vision-Perception-Based RAG for Visually Rich Information Understanding via Iterative Reasoning with Reinforcement Learning
supports_claims: RL-based iterative reasoning with visual perception actions (crop/zoom/search) can improve evidence acquisition in vision-based RAG over visually rich documents.
Integrating retrieval-quality rewards (e.g., NDCG-style) alongside outcome rewards reduces noisy/irrelevant evidence accumulation in multi-turn multimodal RAG.
rationale: VRAG-RL is a NeurIPS 2025 paper that trains VLMs with GRPO to perform iterative search and visual perception actions over visually rich documents, with a fine-grained reward combining retrieval efficiency (NDCG-based), pattern, and model-based outcome rewards. It directly addresses robust evidence construction in multimodal RAG by explicitly penalizing irrelevant retrievals and enabling coarse-to-fine evidence inspection, which connects to the survey's themes of unreliable evidence handling and action control. Best placed as a case study in the multimodal/scenario chapter showing how RL-driven action control supports robust evidence use in vision RAG.
caveat: Focus is on visually rich document QA accuracy; the paper does not explicitly evaluate adversarial or poisoned evidence, so claims about robustness to unreliable evidence should be limited to noisy/irrelevant retrieval rather than adversarial settings.
notes: Code at github.com/Alibaba-NLP/VRAG; benchmarks: SlideVQA, ViDoSeek, MMLongBench.

title: FiD-Light: Efficient and Effective Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
supports_claims: FiD-Light compresses per-passage encoded representations to reduce decoder input length while preserving generation quality, illustrating context compression as an evidence-construction lever for RAG.
Adding textual source pointers and using them to re-rank retrieved passages improves provenance precision and provides attribution signals over many KILT knowledge-intensive tasks.
rationale: The paper proposes an efficient FiD variant that compresses encoded passage vectors before decoding and adds source pointers used as a re-ranker, yielding state-of-the-art KILT scores. For a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence, its main contributions are efficiency and provenance accuracy rather than handling noisy, conflicting, or adversarial evidence, so it is best cited as background on FiD architectures and on attribution/provenance retrieval. It is appropriate for the appendix or background as part of the FiD method lineage rather than as a main mechanistic claim about robustness to unreliable evidence.
caveat: The paper does not explicitly address robustness to noisy, conflicting, or adversarial passages; framing it as evidence-robust would overclaim.

title: ReFIR: Grounding Large Restoration Models with Retrieval Augmentation
supports_claims: RAG concepts extend beyond text to vision/image restoration, where retrieved high-quality references serve as external knowledge to mitigate generative hallucination.
Reference quality and content correlation critically affect RAG outcomes; randomly selected references can degrade performance more than no retrieval at all.
rationale: ReFIR adapts retrieval augmentation to diffusion-based Large Restoration Models, using cross-image injection to incorporate retrieved HQ images and mitigate restoration hallucination. The Table 6 ablation provides relevant insight on unreliable evidence: random references cause substantial degradation while content-correlated ones help, echoing the survey's robustness-to-noise theme. As a vision-modality RAG case it fits the multimodal scenario coverage but lies at the boundary of the survey's core text-RAG focus, warranting appendix-level citation.
caveat: Primarily an image restoration application; robustness-to-unreliable-evidence is a secondary finding, not the central contribution.
notes: Useful as a modality-extension example showing reference quality dependence in non-text RAG.

title: PoisonedEye: Knowledge Poisoning Attack on Retrieval-Augmented Generation based Large Vision-Language Models
supports_claims: Vision-language RAG systems are vulnerable to single-sample knowledge poisoning attacks that manipulate target responses by jointly crafting poison images and texts to satisfy retrievability and inducibility.
Class-targeted multimodal poisoning extends attack reach beyond exact-match queries, and standard defenses like noise, cropping, and RoCLIP only partially mitigate such attacks.
Robust RAG must consider multimodal evidence integrity, since perturbations to retrieval embeddings can cause poisoned image-text pairs to dominate top-K retrieval.
rationale: The paper introduces the first knowledge poisoning attack tailored to vision-language RAG, optimizing poison images so a single injected pair achieves high retrieval and poison success across multiple retrievers and LVLMs. It directly addresses unreliable evidence in multimodal RAG by formalizing retrievability/inducibility properties and demonstrating that existing defenses (noise, crop, RoCLIP) provide limited protection. This is a strong fit for a robust RAG survey's security/integrity section, especially for multimodal scenarios. Overclaim risk: only one poison sample is injected and attacks largely assume white-box retriever access for the strongest variants.
caveat: Strongest variants (PoisonedEye-S/C) assume white-box access to the retriever; evaluation focuses on a single multimodal database (OVEN-Wiki) and a narrow target-response style.
notes: ICML 2025 venue-published; first VLRAG poisoning attack, complementary to PoisonedRAG/TrojanRAG/AgentPoison in the multimodal setting.

title: Retrieval Augmented Zero-Shot Enzyme Generation for Specified Substrate
supports_claims: RAG can be adapted to scientific zero-shot generation tasks like enzyme design by retrieving functionally analogous examples
Domain-specific RAG applications use similarity-based retrieval beyond textual passages
rationale: This paper proposes SENZ, a retrieval-augmented discrete diffusion model for substrate-specified enzyme generation, retrieving enzymes by substrate similarity and using a classifier-guided generator. While it uses RAG terminology, it is a domain-specific protein design application and does not contribute insights on unreliable evidence handling, faithfulness, attribution, robustness under noisy/conflicting passages, action control, or RAG evaluation protocols relevant to the survey. The zero-shot setting addresses absent rather than unreliable evidence, which is a different problem from the survey focus.
caveat: The paper's framing of retrieval over imperfect evidence could be tangentially related, but it does not engage with robustness, faithfulness, or evidence-quality issues central to the survey.

title: RAG-SR: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Neural Symbolic Regression
supports_claims: RAG can mitigate hallucination of small task-specific language models in symbolic/code generation by grounding outputs on a continuously updated library of previously evaluated artifacts.
Retrieval-augmented neural generation extends beyond text to symbolic regression, where retrieved expressions serve as prompts that align generated symbolic trees with desired semantics.
rationale: The paper integrates a retrieval mechanism over a dynamically constructed semantic library with a small Transformer to generate symbolic trees in evolutionary symbolic regression, explicitly framing the retrieval step as hallucination mitigation. It is a niche application of RAG (code/math/symbolic) rather than a study of robust RAG under unreliable evidence; the retrieval pool here is curated and trusted, so it offers no insight into noisy/conflicting/adversarial evidence. It can still be cited in an appendix to show that retrieval-based grounding generalizes across modalities and lightweight model regimes.
caveat: Does not address unreliable/conflicting/poisoned evidence or attribution; 'hallucination' here means semantically off-target symbolic trees, not factual unfaithfulness in QA.

title: REAR: A Relevance-Aware Retrieval-Augmented Framework for Open-Domain Question Answering
supports_claims: Explicit relevance-assessment modules integrated into RAG architectures can mitigate LLM susceptibility to irrelevant or noisy retrieved documents.
Bi-granularity (coarse binary plus fine-grained preference) relevance supervision combined with noise-resistant training improves adaptive use of parametric versus external knowledge.
Relevance-aware generation enables knowledge-consistency verification between parametric and retrieved evidence for more reliable answer selection.
rationale: REAR adds an explicit relevance-assessment module to an LLM-based RAG pipeline and trains it with bi-granularity relevance fusion plus noise-resistant objectives so the model can adaptively rely on internal or external knowledge depending on document reliability. This directly addresses the survey's core question of how LLMs should behave under unreliable retrieved evidence, with quantitative gains on four open-domain QA benchmarks and explicit comparisons to Self-RAG and RobustLM. It is a venue-published EMNLP 2024 paper with code, making it a strong main-text reference in the model-evidence-use lineage. Overclaim risk is moderate: results are limited to open-domain QA and document-level (not sentence/token-level) relevance.
caveat: Evaluation is restricted to open-domain QA at document granularity; generalization to other knowledge-intensive tasks and finer-grained evidence is untested.
notes: ACL Anthology entry 2024.emnlp-main.321; code at github.com/RUCAIBox/REAR.

title: ReDeEP: Detecting Hallucination in Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Mechanistic Interpretability
supports_claims: RAG models can hallucinate even when retrieved evidence is accurate and relevant, due to overreliance on parametric knowledge in later-layer FFNs and insufficient retention of external context by copying attention heads.
Mechanistic interpretability can decouple a model's use of external evidence versus parametric knowledge, providing diagnostic signals for hallucination detection in RAG.
Detection-time interventions that reweight attention heads and FFN contributions can mitigate hallucinations without parameter updates.
rationale: ReDeEP investigates the internal mechanisms behind RAG hallucinations when retrieved evidence is accurate, identifying that Knowledge FFNs over-inject parametric knowledge while Copying Heads fail to retain external context. It proposes detection (ReDeEP) and mitigation (AARF) methods validated on RAGTruth and Dolly (AC) with LLaMA models, directly addressing model faithfulness to evidence under conditions where retrieval is correct but the model still drifts. This is a venue-backbone contribution for the model_evidence_use perspective in a robust-RAG survey, distinguishing RAG hallucination from knowledge conflict and offering both diagnostic and corrective tools.
caveat: Experiments focus on LLaMA-2/3 families and assume accurate retrieved context, so generalization to noisy/adversarial retrieval and larger or non-decoder architectures is not fully demonstrated.
notes: Strong mechanistic interpretability contribution; pairs well with citations on knowledge conflict, hallucination detection (SelfCheckGPT, EigenScore), and RAGTruth benchmark.

title: RealRAG: Retrieval-augmented Realistic Image Generation via Self-reflective Contrastive Learning
supports_claims: Retrieval based purely on similarity may surface evidence redundant with what the generator already knows, motivating retrievers that target missing knowledge.
RAG can be extended to multimodal generation (text-to-image) to mitigate hallucination on fine-grained and unseen novel objects.
rationale: RealRAG proposes a self-reflective contrastive retriever for text-to-image generation that intentionally retrieves images outside the generator's existing generation space, addressing a form of evidence-utility mismatch in RAG. While the work targets image generation rather than the LLM-based RAG that is the survey's main focus, it offers a useful boundary case showing how unreliable/redundant retrievals can fail to compensate for model knowledge gaps. Placement in an extended/multimodal appendix avoids overclaiming its direct relevance to text-based unreliable-evidence robustness.
caveat: Scope is text-to-image generation, not text-based RAG; reliability framing differs from typical noisy-evidence settings, and only a project page is referenced without confirmed code release.
notes: Boundary multimodal RAG paper; cite as evidence that retrieval-utility mismatch matters across modalities.

title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
supports_claims: Self-reflection tokens enable adaptive retrieval and on-demand grounding decisions, improving robustness when evidence is unnecessary or unreliable.
Critique tokens for relevance and support provide a fine-grained mechanism to filter retrieved passages and enforce faithfulness during decoding.
Controllable inference via weighted reflection-token scoring allows trading off citation precision, fluency, and retrieval frequency at test time.
rationale: Self-RAG trains an LM to emit reflection tokens that decide when to retrieve, assess passage relevance (IsRel), verify support (IsSup), and rate utility (IsUse), then uses segment-level beam search weighted by these scores. This is a canonical mechanism for action control and grounding under potentially irrelevant or unsupportive evidence, directly addressing key axes of robust RAG. Main-text citation in the action-control section is appropriate, with cross-reference to evidence use and faithfulness. Caveat: relies on GPT-4-distilled critic labels and Wikipedia retrieval, so robustness to adversarial or poisoned evidence is not directly evaluated.
caveat: Reflection tokens are distilled from GPT-4 judgments and the method is not directly evaluated against adversarial or poisoned retrieval contexts.
notes: Widely cited ICLR 2024 backbone for adaptive/self-reflective RAG.

title: Retrieval augmented text-to-SQL generation for epidemiological question answering using electronic health records
supports_claims: RAG with in-domain question-SQL demonstrations improves text-to-SQL accuracy over static prompting in biomedical EHR settings.
Domain-specific RAG applications in healthcare highlight the need for medical entity normalization and ontology grounding alongside retrieval.
rationale: The paper applies RAG to text-to-SQL generation over EHR/claims databases using the OMOP-CDM, integrating a medical coding step and showing that retrieving similar question-SQL pairs significantly improves accuracy across multiple LLMs. It is primarily an applied domain study, not a robustness or unreliable-evidence contribution, but it provides a useful boundary example of domain-specific RAG with structured data and ontology grounding. Appendix citation fits coverage of biomedical/structured-data scenarios without overclaiming on robustness insights.
caveat: Limited dataset size and no analysis of noisy/conflicting retrieval; does not directly address unreliable evidence or adversarial robustness.
notes: Released dataset and code on GitHub; useful as a scenario case for domain RAG over EHRs.

title: Reliable Decision‑Making via Calibration‑Oriented Retrieval‑Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Calibration-oriented reranking can align RAG confidence with empirical decision correctness, mitigating overconfidence when retrieved evidence is unreliable.
Training a forecasting function over query-document pairs enables selective retrieval and query reformulation when no candidate passage provides sufficient decision support.
rationale: CalibRAG proposes a forecasting function f(t,q,d) trained with self-consistency soft labels to predict whether a user's decision based on retrieved evidence will be correct, then uses it both to rerank documents and to abstain/reformulate when confidence falls below a threshold. This directly addresses unreliable retrieval (top-1 documents that mislead) and overconfident RAG outputs, which are core concerns of the survey. It belongs in the action-control section because the central contribution is calibration-driven routing and adaptive retrieval rather than retrieval quality per se. The approach is validated on general QA and medical MIRAGE benchmarks against calibration tuning, verbalized confidence, reranking, and Self-RAG baselines.
caveat: Relies on a surrogate LLM user model and GPT-4o-mini grading, so calibration claims depend on these proxies; synthetic supervision generation adds nontrivial overhead.
notes: NeurIPS 2025 venue-linked; strong fit for the action-control/calibration thread of the survey.

title: Speculative RAG: Enhancing Retrieval Augmented Generation through Drafting
supports_claims: Drafting answers from diverse document subsets and verifying via a generalist LM mitigates position bias and improves grounding in RAG.
Rationale-based verification scores (self-consistency and self-reflection) can be used to select reliable answer drafts when retrieved evidence is noisy or redundant.
rationale: Speculative RAG decomposes RAG into a specialist drafter generating multiple rationale-grounded drafts from clustered document subsets and a generalist verifier that scores drafts via self-consistency and self-reflection. This is relevant to robust RAG because multi-perspective sampling reduces redundancy and the verifier acts as a selection/abstention-like mechanism over candidate answers, both useful angles for handling unreliable evidence. However, the paper primarily targets efficiency and accuracy on clean QA benchmarks rather than explicitly studying noisy, poisoned, or conflicting evidence, so it best fits as supporting coverage in an appendix rather than a core mechanistic reference.
caveat: Does not explicitly evaluate under adversarial, conflicting, or unreliable evidence conditions; gains are demonstrated on standard QA benchmarks.
notes: ICLR 2025 published; could also be cited under evidence_construction for multi-perspective clustering.

title: MMed-RAG: Versatile Multimodal RAG System for Medical Vision Language Models
supports_claims: Multimodal medical RAG systems must handle domain heterogeneity via domain-aware retrievers and adaptively select the number of retrieved contexts to avoid noise-induced hallucinations.

Preference fine-tuning targeting cross-modality alignment and over-reliance on retrieved evidence mitigates two distinct RAG failure modes (copy-reference and retrieval interference) in vision-language models.
Diagnostic metrics such as Copy-Reference rate and Over-Reliance rate provide useful evaluation tools for measuring RAG robustness under unreliable retrieved evidence.
rationale: MMed-RAG is an ICLR 2025 multimodal medical RAG system that explicitly identifies and mitigates two failure modes induced by unreliable retrieved evidence: cross-modality misalignment (model copies retrieved text while ignoring the image) and over-reliance interference (correct answers flipped to wrong by noisy retrieval). It contributes adaptive context selection via similarity-gap thresholding, domain-aware retriever routing, and RAG-based DPO with constructed preference pairs, plus theoretical analysis of weight shifts. These contributions directly support the survey's main claims on robust RAG under unreliable evidence in the multimodal/medical scenario, justifying main_cite placement in the modality section.
caveat: Scope is limited to medical VLMs and the preference-pair construction depends on the base model already producing some correct vs. incorrect responses; generalization beyond medical imaging is not fully validated.
notes: Strong candidate as a venue-backbone reference for multimodal RAG with unreliable evidence and as evaluation reference for CR/OR diagnostics.

title: Generate-then-Ground in Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Multi-hop Question Answering
supports_claims: Generate-then-ground frameworks can mitigate noise in retrieved documents by alternating LLM answer generation with evidence-based revision.
Batch grounding strategies and instructional grounding distillation help LLMs ignore plausible-looking but irrelevant retrieved content in multi-hop QA.
rationale: The paper proposes GenGround, an alternative to retrieve-then-read that first generates an answer from parametric knowledge then grounds and revises it using retrieved evidence, explicitly targeting noise and irrelevant content in retrieved documents. It also introduces a batch grounding strategy and instructional grounding distillation for smaller models, with experiments on four multi-hop QA benchmarks. This is directly relevant to robust RAG under unreliable evidence and knowledge conflict between parametric and retrieved sources, making it suitable for the model-evidence-use section. Overclaim risk is modest since the approach still depends on LLM judgment of evidence relevance.
caveat: Evaluation is limited to multi-hop QA with Wikipedia corpora and does not explicitly stress-test adversarial or counterfactual noise beyond standard retrieval imperfections.

title: Benchmarking Multimodal Retrieval Augmented Generation with Dynamic VQA Dataset and Self-adaptive Planning Agent
supports_claims: Heuristic multimodal RAG with fixed two-step retrieval fails on dynamic, multi-hop, or multimodal-knowledge questions because of non-adaptive and overloaded retrieval queries.

Self-adaptive planning agents that decompose complex multimodal questions into sub-question chains and dynamically choose retrieval tools (image/text search) improve robustness over rigid mRAG pipelines.
Dyn-VQA provides a benchmark for evaluating mRAG under rapidly changing answers, cross-modal knowledge needs, and >2-hop reasoning.
rationale: The paper introduces Dyn-VQA, a benchmark targeting dynamic/multimodal/multi-hop questions that expose rigidity failures of heuristic mRAG, and proposes OmniSearch, a self-adaptive planning agent that interleaves sub-question decomposition with tool-conditioned retrieval and feedback. This directly supports a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence by giving both a multimodal evaluation lens and an action-control mechanism that re-routes retrieval when evidence is stale, ambiguous, or insufficient. Placement in the modality/scenario chapter is natural, with secondary support for adaptive-retrieval (action control) and evaluation sections. Overclaim risk: results are largely tied to GPT-4V/Qwen-VL backbones and Google-based retrieval tools, so generality of the agent design beyond these tools is not fully established.
caveat: Evaluation depends on commercial search APIs and proprietary MLLM backbones; F1-recall metric and small benchmark size (~1.5K) limit statistical robustness.

title: Think-on-Graph 2.0: Deep and Faithful Large Language Model Reasoning with Knowledge-guided Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Tight-coupling of KG-based and text-based retrieval through iterative graph-guided context retrieval improves multi-hop reasoning faithfulness and reduces hallucination compared to loose-coupling hybrid RAG.
Iterative knowledge-guided retrieval with context-based entity pruning enables deeper evidence gathering for complex knowledge-intensive QA tasks.
rationale: ToG-2 proposes a hybrid KG+text RAG framework that iteratively performs graph search guided by contextual document retrieval, addressing both the incompleteness of KGs and the lack of structured relations in text-only RAG. It directly contributes to the modality/scenario dimension of robust RAG by showing how structured knowledge can guide more faithful context retrieval, with explicit discussion of hallucination mitigation and refusal behavior. Suitable for the main modality section as a representative graph/KG-augmented RAG approach. Overclaim risk is moderate since improvements depend on KG completeness, which the authors themselves analyze in ablations.
caveat: Performance depends on KG completeness and entity linking quality; the framework is training-free but adds significant runtime and API cost overhead compared to vanilla RAG.

title: Boosting the Potential of Large Language Models with an Intelligent Information Assistant
supports_claims: Assistant-based RAG architectures can decouple retrieval/decision logic from a frozen main LLM, using planning steps to assess usefulness of retrieved memory and knowledge before injection.
Curriculum learning combined with DPO can align an auxiliary retrieval/extraction module with downstream LLM preferences, improving noise filtering and reducing irrelevant evidence.
rationale: AssistRAG introduces a trainable assistant that performs query decomposition, knowledge extraction, and explicit planning steps to decide whether retrieved memory or knowledge is useful before passing it to the main LLM. This relevance assessment and filtering mechanism connects to action control and evidence construction in robust RAG, particularly for handling noisy or unreliable retrieved evidence. The paper is venue-linked (NeurIPS 2024) with code, but its main contribution is system-level rather than a focused study of unreliable evidence robustness, so appendix-level citation is appropriate.
caveat: The paper does not systematically study adversarial or unreliable evidence; its 'usefulness' planner is evaluated only on standard multi-hop QA, so robustness claims under truly noisy/poisoned retrieval are not directly supported.

title: ChatQA 2: Bridging the Gap to Proprietary LLMs in Long Context and RAG Capabilities
supports_claims: Long-context LLMs combined with RAG can outperform direct long-context solutions when sufficient top-k chunks are retrieved, showing complementarity between RAG and long context.
RAG performance with long-context retrievers can be robust to chunk size variations and improves with more retrieved tokens.
rationale: The paper presents ChatQA 2, an open Llama3-based 128K context model with extensive comparison between RAG and long-context solutions across ultra-long, long, and short benchmarks. While it does not directly target unreliable evidence, noise, or attacks, it provides useful empirical evidence on RAG robustness to chunk size and the tradeoff between retrieval count and generation quality, relevant to evidence construction choices in long-context RAG. Best placed as appendix support for the long-context RAG scenario discussion, not as a main mechanistic robustness contribution.
caveat: Focused on capability/accuracy benchmarks rather than robustness under noisy, conflicting, or adversarial evidence; overclaiming reliability contributions should be avoided.
notes: ICLR 2025; open-sourced weights, data, and evaluation setup at chatqa2-project.github.io.

title: SV-RAG: LoRA-Contextualizing Adaptation of  MLLMs for Long Document Understanding
supports_claims: Multimodal RAG with MLLM-based evidence page retrieval can scale long visually-rich document QA by filtering irrelevant pages before answer generation.
Dual LoRA adapters on a shared MLLM backbone allow joint retrieval and QA specialization, addressing efficiency and relevance bottlenecks in visual long-document RAG.
rationale: SV-RAG proposes a self-visual RAG framework where an MLLM with dual LoRA adapters performs both evidence page retrieval and QA over long visually-rich documents, using contextualized late interaction. It is directly relevant as a scenario-specific (vision/long-document) RAG method showing how retrieving relevant pages reduces noise and memory burden compared to feeding all pages. It fits the modality_scenario_core section as supporting evidence that retrieval design matters for reliability in multimodal long-document RAG, though it focuses more on efficiency/accuracy than on adversarial or unreliable-evidence robustness.
caveat: The paper does not directly study unreliable evidence, knowledge conflict, or adversarial robustness; it mainly addresses efficiency and retrieval accuracy for visual long documents.
notes: Only PaddleOCR repo referenced in extracted text; no clear release of SV-RAG code/data found in excerpt.

title: Understanding Parametric and Contextual Knowledge Reconciliation within Large Language Models
