It introduces WebPuzzle, a benchmark explicitly designed to require evidence gathering, conflict resolution, verification/denoising, and reflective correction, which maps cleanly to the survey's robust-RAG-under-unreliable-evidence theme. Suitable as a main_cite under action_control (adaptive retrieval/routing) with a secondary tie to evaluation. Overclaim risk: results are primarily Chinese 7B-scale and rely on LLM-as-judge graders.
caveat: Evaluation is heavily Chinese-centric, uses LLM-based graders, and reward design choices may confound the claimed emergence of search-intensity scaling.
notes: NeurIPS 2025 venue-linked; code/data not yet released at submission.

title: Leveraging Uncertainty Estimates To Improve Classifier Performance
supports_claims: Uncertainty estimates can improve decision boundaries beyond score-only thresholding, motivating uncertainty-aware abstention/control in downstream pipelines.
Score estimation bias systematically depends on uncertainty, supporting calibration-aware action policies.
rationale: This ICLR 2024 paper provides theoretical and algorithmic analysis of leveraging uncertainty estimates to improve binary classifier decision boundaries, including NP-hardness results and DP/isotonic-regression algorithms. It does not address retrieval-augmented generation, evidence quality, or any RAG-specific mechanism; experiments are on CTR and e-commerce classification datasets. It is at most a background reference for uncertainty/calibration foundations that could justify abstention or routing policies in robust RAG, but it does not directly support any main claim about unreliable evidence.
caveat: No RAG, retrieval, generation, or evidence-quality content; relevance is only via the general uncertainty-for-decisions foundation. Risk of overclaim if cited as RAG-specific.
notes: Scenario tag 'code_math_symbolic' from metadata appears to be a mislabel; paper is tabular binary classification.

title: Neural Graph Matching Improves Retrieval Augmented Generation in Molecular Machine Learning
supports_claims: Naive RAG concatenation can fail or hurt performance in structured scientific tasks, motivating explicit alignment between retrieved and target evidence.
Neural graph matching offers a noise-robust mechanism for aligning retrieved structural evidence to the query, providing graceful degradation when retrieved references are only partially similar.
rationale: The paper introduces MARASON, a retrieval-augmented mass spectrum simulator that uses neural graph matching to align retrieved molecular fragments to target fragments, showing that naive concatenation-based RAG fails while learned matching is more robust to noisy/imperfect retrieved evidence. It also analyzes when retrieval helps versus hurts based on Tanimoto similarity thresholds, which is a useful robustness insight for the survey. However, the application is narrow (molecular MS/MS simulation, not LLM-based RAG), so an appendix or extended modality discussion is the appropriate placement rather than a main citation. Overclaim risk: this is not a text/LLM RAG method and its lessons may not directly transfer.
caveat: Domain-specific (small-molecule mass spectra) and not LLM-based RAG; insights about matching-based robustness must be carefully framed when generalized.
notes: ICML 2025 (PMLR v267); code available at github.com/coleygroup/ms-pred.

title: RAG-SR: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Neural Symbolic Regression
supports_claims: RAG can mitigate hallucination in domain-specific generation tasks by grounding outputs in a retrieved library of evaluated expressions.
In symbolic/math scenarios, retrieval-augmented neural generation can outperform purely retrieval-based or purely generative baselines.
rationale: The paper proposes RAG-SR, which uses a retrieval-augmented neural network to generate symbolic trees aligned with desired semantics, explicitly framing retrieval as a hallucination-mitigation mechanism for an online-trained language model. This is a venue-published (ICLR 2025) instance of RAG applied to the code/math/symbolic scenario, providing useful coverage for a survey section on RAG in non-text modalities. However, the retrieval setting (semantic library of evolved trees) and unreliability framing are quite specialized, so it is best placed in appendix/extended coverage rather than as a main mechanistic reference.
caveat: Hallucination here is narrowly defined as grammatically correct but semantically mismatched symbolic trees; insights may not transfer directly to standard text-based RAG under unreliable evidence.
notes: Code available at https://github.com/hengzhe-zhang/RAG-SR

title: BSharedRAG: Backbone Shared Retrieval-Augmented Generation for the E-commerce Domain
supports_claims: Domain-specific RAG can benefit from sharing a continually pre-trained backbone between retriever and generator via task-specific LoRA modules, avoiding negative transfer.
High-quality domain corpora and QDA construction reduce noise/conflict issues present in user-generated review-based knowledge bases for e-commerce QA.
rationale: The paper proposes a backbone-shared RAG architecture (BSharedRAG) and a curated WorthBuying e-commerce dataset, addressing how separate vs. fully-shared retrieval/generation training affect domain adaptation. It only tangentially touches on unreliable evidence by motivating dataset cleaning to mitigate noisy/conflicting user-generated reviews, but its main contribution is architectural and dataset-centric rather than focused on robustness to unreliable retrieved evidence, attribution, or abstention. It is reasonable to cite as boundary coverage of domain-specific RAG architectures in an appendix, but not as a main pillar of the survey.
caveat: Does not directly evaluate robustness to noisy/conflicting retrieved evidence, attacks, or calibration; overclaiming relevance to unreliable-evidence robustness would be unwarranted.
notes: Artifacts available at https://bsharedrag.github.io; mainly a domain RAG architecture paper for e-commerce.

title: SeRTS: Self-Rewarding Tree Search for Biomedical Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Tree-search-based adaptive query reformulation can improve retrieval quality for domain-specific RAG when single-shot retrieval is insufficient.
Self-rewarding LLM evaluators combined with PPO fine-tuning can iteratively refine retrieval policies in biomedical RAG settings.
rationale: SeRTS proposes a Monte Carlo Tree Search plus self-rewarding paradigm for adaptive query reformulation in biomedical RAG, fine-tuned via PPO using BM25 retrieval feedback. It contributes to evidence construction and adaptive retrieval control, but is narrowly scoped to biomedical QA on BioASQ and does not directly study unreliable or adversarial evidence. It fits as appendix support for domain-specific adaptive retrieval methods rather than a main mechanism for robust RAG under unreliable evidence.
caveat: Limited to biomedical domain with BM25 and a single PPO iteration; does not evaluate robustness to noisy, conflicting, or poisoned evidence.
notes: EMNLP 2024 Findings; uses LLama2-7B-chat and GPT-3.5-Turbo on BioASQ Task 11b.

title: Constructing Confidence Intervals for Average Treatment Effects from Multiple Datasets
supports_claims: Not applicable - the paper addresses causal inference (ATE confidence intervals from multiple observational datasets via prediction-powered inference) and has no connection to retrieval-augmented generation.
rationale: This is a statistical causal inference paper that proposes a method for constructing valid confidence intervals for average treatment effects from multiple observational datasets using prediction-powered inference, applied to medical examples (MIMIC-III, COVID-19 data). It does not involve retrieval, generation, language models, multimodal inputs, or any RAG-related mechanisms beyond a brief mention of LLMs as possible future work. There is no methodological or empirical contribution relevant to robust RAG under unreliable evidence.
caveat: The paper was likely auto-tagged into a multimodal_rag_100 collection due to the biomedical domain tag, but it has no substantive RAG relevance.
notes: Pure causal inference / statistics paper; off-topic for the survey.

title: Generative Retrieval Meets Multi-Graded Relevance
supports_claims: Generative retrieval can model multi-graded relevance via constrained contrastive training over learned document identifiers.
Docid design must balance semantic relevance with distinctness to support fine-grained ranking.
rationale: This paper proposes GR2, a generative retrieval framework that produces document identifiers directly via encoder-decoder models with multi-graded relevance signals. It addresses ranking effectiveness within the generative-retrieval paradigm rather than retrieval-augmented generation, and does not engage with unreliable evidence, faithfulness, abstention, robustness to noisy contexts, or any multimodal/agentic scenario relevant to the survey. Its contributions concern docid construction and learning losses for IR effectiveness, not robust RAG mechanisms.
caveat: Despite being tagged under a multimodal RAG collection, the paper is purely text IR and contributes no evidence on RAG robustness or unreliable-evidence handling.
notes: Venue: NeurIPS 2024; concerns generative IR, not RAG.

title: ReliabilityRAG: Effective and Provably Robust Defense for RAG-based Web-Search
supports_claims: Reliability-aware document selection via Maximum Independent Set over a contradiction graph provides provably robust defense against corpus poisoning and prompt injection in RAG.
Weighted sample-and-aggregate frameworks leveraging document ranking/weights enable scalable robustness against adversarial retrieval corruption while preserving benign utility.
Defense-in-depth strategies that exploit retriever reliability signals outperform position-agnostic robust RAG baselines on both short-form QA and long-form generation.
rationale: This NeurIPS 2025 paper proposes ReliabilityRAG, which constructs a contradiction graph over retrieved documents (via NLI on isolated answers) and selects a rank-aware Maximum Independent Set to filter malicious passages, with provable robustness guarantees and a weighted sample-and-aggregate variant for scalability. It directly targets unreliable evidence (corpus poisoning, prompt injection) and benchmarks against RobustRAG, AstuteRAG, and InstructRAG on RQA/NQ/TQA/Bio, making it a backbone reference for the security/integrity dimension of robust RAG. Main-text security placement is appropriate because it advances both the mechanism (consistency-based filtering with reliability priors) and the evaluation lineage for defended RAG.
caveat: Robustness guarantees depend on NLI quality and the assumption that malicious answers diverge enough to be detected as contradictions; effectiveness on truly adaptive context-aware attacks and very long-form generation remains less explored.
notes: Code release promised post-acceptance; only a partial HuggingFace URL signal extracted.

title: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Medicine
supports_claims: Domain-specific RAG benchmarks (e.g., MIRAGE for medicine) reveal that retriever/corpus/LLM choices have large and task-dependent effects on answer accuracy.

Medical RAG exhibits log-linear scaling with the number of retrieved snippets and a 'lost-in-the-middle' effect on the position of the ground-truth snippet, highlighting context-use robustness issues.
Combining heterogeneous corpora and fusing retrievers (e.g., RRF) tends to improve robustness across diverse medical QA tasks.
rationale: The paper proposes MIRAGE, a benchmark of 7,663 medical QA items, and MedRAG, a toolkit spanning 5 corpora, 4 retrievers, and 6 LLMs, enabling systematic evaluation of RAG component choices. It documents log-linear scaling with retrieved-snippet count and a 'lost-in-the-middle' phenomenon in medical RAG, both directly relevant to robust RAG under unreliable/noisy evidence. As a venue-published (ACL Findings 2024) benchmark with open code and data covering a high-stakes domain, it fits main-text evaluation citation, particularly in the domain/scenario section.
caveat: The work focuses on multi-choice medical QA with vanilla prepend-RAG, so its conclusions may not transfer to open-ended generation, adversarial/poisoned evidence, or non-medical domains.
notes: ACL Findings 2024; strong fit for evaluation and domain-scenario discussion in survey.

title: Unleash Model Capacity for Universal Dense Retrieval by Task Specialty Optimization
supports_claims: Multi-task dense retrieval can be improved via task-specialty optimization that adjusts parameter learning rates based on task sensitivity
Universal retrieval bottleneck is parameter optimization rather than model capacity
rationale: This paper proposes TACO-DR, a multi-task optimization method (T-SAGE) for universal dense retrieval on KILT, focusing on parameter sensitivity-based learning rate adjustment to capture task-specific signals. It addresses retrieval accuracy across multiple knowledge-intensive tasks but does not engage with robustness to unreliable evidence, noise filtering, adversarial conditions, faithfulness, or action control in RAG. The contribution is on dense retriever training optimization rather than any of the survey's core perspectives. Including it would dilute focus without adding evidence for robust-RAG claims.
caveat: While dense retrieval is foundational to RAG, this paper's multi-task optimization focus does not address evidence reliability or any robustness dimension central to the survey.
notes: Scenario tag code_math_symbolic appears mismatched; the paper actually evaluates on KILT knowledge-intensive tasks (QA, fact check, entity linking, slot filling, dialog).

title: On the Vulnerability of Applying Retrieval-Augmented Generation within Knowledge-Intensive Application Domains
supports_claims: Dense retrieval systems in domain-specific RAG (medical and legal Q&A) are vulnerable to universal poisoning attacks where attacker-crafted documents are reliably retrieved for targeted queries across diverse corpora, retrievers, and query sets.

An orthogonal augmentation property of dense retrievers explains why concatenating targeted content to queries preserves high similarity, motivating Mahalanobis-distance-based detection that outperforms L2-norm baselines for filtering poisoned documents.
rationale: This ICML 2025 paper systematically demonstrates RAG corpus poisoning vulnerabilities across 225 setups in medical Q&A (and legal Q&A), introduces a theoretical explanation via orthogonal augmentation, and proposes a shrinkage-regularized Mahalanobis distance defense with near-perfect detection rates. It directly contributes to the security/integrity dimension of robust RAG under unreliable evidence, with a strong domain-specific (biomed/legal) scenario focus. Placement in the security section is appropriate because it spans both attack characterization and defense design.
caveat: Defense assumes access to a clean anchor set of documents tied to protected queries, and PubMed subset rather than full corpus is used; generalization to non-medical adversarial scenarios is only lightly explored.
notes: Strong venue-backbone citation for the security/poisoning subsection; also relevant as a domain-specific (biomed/legal) case study.

title: HyPA-RAG: A Hybrid Parameter Adaptive Retrieval-Augmented Generation System for AI Legal and Policy Applications
supports_claims: Hybrid retrieval combining dense, sparse, and knowledge graph methods with adaptive parameter selection can improve faithfulness and correctness in domain-specific legal RAG
Query complexity classifiers enable adaptive retrieval configurations that mitigate common RAG failure points in high-stakes domains
rationale: The paper proposes HyPA-RAG, a hybrid RAG system for AI legal/policy QA on NYC Local Law 144, combining dense+sparse+KG retrieval with a query complexity classifier that adaptively tunes top-k and rewrites. It is relevant to a robust-RAG survey for its domain-specific application, adaptive parameter control, and an evaluation framework using custom legal question types and RAGAS-style metrics. Placement in appendix is appropriate because the contribution is narrow (single law corpus) and the workshop scope limits generality, but it provides useful evidence on domain-specific reliability and adaptive retrieval.
caveat: Evaluated on a single 15-page legal corpus (LL144) with one human evaluator, limiting generalizability and statistical robustness of the reliability claims.
notes: ACL Anthology workshop paper (CustomNLP4U 2024); code and dataset available on GitHub.

title: Knowledge-Consistent Dialogue Generation with Language Models and Knowledge Graphs
supports_claims: KG-based RAG benefits from learned subgraph retrieval that filters irrelevant facts before generation, addressing noisy evidence in knowledge-grounded dialogue.
Graph-text contrastive learning can enforce faithful use of retrieved evidence and reduce hallucination in generated responses.
Standard text overlap metrics are insufficient for evaluating knowledge faithfulness; QA-based metrics like KQA better assess factual consistency.
rationale: SURGE proposes an end-to-end KG-RAG framework for dialogue that retrieves context-relevant subgraphs (filtering ~87% irrelevant facts), encodes them with invariant graph encoding, and uses graph-text contrastive learning to enforce faithful grounding. It directly addresses unreliable/noisy evidence in graph-based RAG and proposes a knowledge-verifying QA metric for faithfulness, which is relevant to both evidence construction and model evidence use perspectives. It fits as a representative KG-RAG scenario example in the modality section, though it does not address adversarial poisoning or broader unreliable-evidence robustness.
caveat: Scope is limited to dialogue with a curated KG; unreliability is framed as irrelevant facts rather than adversarial or conflicting evidence, so over-claiming broader robustness should be avoided.
notes: ICLR 2023 under review version; verify final publication status when adding bibtex.

title: RECOMP: Improving Retrieval-Augmented LMs with Context Compression and Selective Augmentation
supports_claims: Context compression of retrieved documents can filter irrelevant evidence and reduce LM distraction while maintaining task performance.
Selective augmentation (returning an empty summary when retrieved evidence is unhelpful) is an effective mechanism for handling unreliable retrieval results.
Compressors trained with end-task signals can outperform off-the-shelf summarization for RAG and transfer across different LMs.
rationale: RECOMP proposes both extractive and abstractive compressors that summarize retrieved documents before prepending them to the LM input, with explicit selective augmentation (empty summary) when retrieved evidence is irrelevant or harmful. This directly addresses two key axes of robust RAG under unreliable evidence: filtering noisy/irrelevant retrieval and abstaining from augmentation when retrieval hurts. The analyses on faithfulness, comprehensiveness, and how models copy spans even when answer is absent are particularly useful for the evidence-construction chapter, and the work is a venue-backbone for context-compression lineage. Placement under main:evidence is appropriate, with possible cross-reference to action_control for the selective augmentation aspect.
caveat: Selective augmentation here is binary (summary vs. empty) and tied to specific base LMs; transfer experiments show limited generalization for QA across LM families, so claims about general robustness should be tempered.
notes: ICLR 2024, code at github.com/carriex/recomp; relevant for both evidence construction (compression/filtering) and adaptive/selective augmentation discussions.

title: NutriBench: A Dataset for Evaluating Large Language Models in Nutrition Estimation from Meal Descriptions
supports_claims: Domain-specific RAG benchmarks reveal that retrieval alignment with query format (e.g., natural vs metric serving sizes) is critical for usefulness of retrieved evidence.
In high-stakes biomedical/nutrition tasks, RAG does not always improve over CoT and can mislead strong models when retrieved context is misaligned or noisy.
rationale: NutriBench is an ICLR 2025 benchmark that evaluates 12 LLMs on carbohydrate estimation using Base, CoT, RAG, and RAG+CoT prompting, with a real-world diabetes risk simulation. It provides concrete evidence that RAG can fail to help (and even hurt) when the retrieval database's format (metric 100g servings) is misaligned with query phrasing (natural servings), which is a relevant unreliable-evidence failure mode for a robust RAG survey. Placement in appendix is appropriate because the paper's primary contribution is a domain benchmark rather than a RAG method or robustness technique, but it offers a useful case for evaluation coverage in biomedical scenarios.
caveat: Primarily a nutrition benchmark; RAG analysis is limited to a small number of models and a single retrieval setup, so claims about robust RAG should not overgeneralize from this paper.
notes: Artifacts: project page, GitHub simulator, HuggingFace model linked.

title: FiD-Light: Efficient and Effective Retrieval-Augmented Text Generation
supports_claims: FiD-style architectures can be made more efficient by compressing per-passage encoder vectors before decoding while preserving downstream effectiveness on knowledge-intensive tasks.
Source pointer mechanisms integrated into FiD enable joint generation and re-ranking, improving provenance precision on KILT tasks.
rationale: The paper introduces FiD-Light, an efficiency-focused FiD variant that compresses encoder outputs before decoding and adds source-pointer-based re-ranking for provenance attribution on KILT tasks. While not directly about unreliable evidence robustness, it contributes to the lineage of context construction and provenance attribution in RAG, which underpins many robust-RAG mechanisms. It is best placed in an appendix as a foundational architectural reference rather than a main mechanistic citation, since it does not address noise, conflict, poisoning, or abstention.
caveat: Focus is efficiency and provenance precision, not robustness to unreliable or adversarial evidence; overclaiming relevance to reliability would be misleading.
notes: Scenario hint code_math_symbolic seems mislabeled; this is more long-context document QA/KILT.

title: Position: Retrieval-augmented systems can be dangerous medical communicators
supports_claims: Even when RAG systems retrieve and cite accurate sources, generated responses can be pragmatically misleading by decontextualizing facts, omitting critical evidence, and reinforcing user biases.

Domain-specific (medical) query analysis exposes failure modes of citation-grounded systems that traditional factuality/relevance metrics fail to capture, motivating new evaluation protocols for pragmatic alignment.
Robust RAG must reason about query intent, source intent, and downstream consequences of generated text, not just retrieve and cite verbatim.
rationale: This ICML 2025 position paper conducts a large-scale empirical analysis of Google AI Overview and Perplexity on 178 medical queries (disputed diagnoses, procedure safety/complications), demonstrating that RAG systems can be 'narrowly accurate but pragmatically misaligned' — confirming biases, decontextualizing facts, and ignoring source intent. It is highly relevant as a case study of unreliable evidence use in a high-stakes domain, and the proposed benchmark direction on pragmatic misalignment supports the evaluation side of the survey. Best placed as a domain case study illustrating how factual-grounding metrics underestimate real-world reliability risks.
caveat: Position paper rather than a methodological contribution; empirical analysis is limited to two commercial systems and ~178 queries with LLM-as-judge evaluation, so findings are illustrative rather than systematically comparable across RAG methods.
notes: PMLR v267 (ICML 2025); released artifact at github.com/rayarxti/rag-medical-communicator.

title: Two-tiered Encoder-based Hallucination Detection for Retrieval-Augmented Generation in the Wild
supports_claims: Lightweight encoder-based NLI classifiers can effectively detect ungrounded LLM responses in industrial RAG, often outperforming prompted or fine-tuned decoder LLMs.
Distinguishing verifiable from non-verifiable (small talk) statements via a two-tier pipeline improves hallucination flagging precision in customer-service RAG.
rationale: The paper proposes RAGHalu, a two-tier DeBERTa encoder classifier that first separates verifiable from non-verifiable LLM utterances and then judges KB-grounded support, evaluated on four enterprise customer-service brands plus public hallucination benchmarks. It is directly relevant to robust RAG under unreliable evidence on the faithfulness/grounding-detection axis, and provides industrial cost/latency considerations and an annotated dataset that aid coverage. Appendix placement fits because the contribution is an applied detector rather than a foundational mechanism or evaluation benchmark for the survey's core taxonomy. The scenario label of code_math_symbolic in the metadata is incorrect; the actual domain is customer-service dialogue.
caveat: Industry-specific customer-service focus and small brand datasets limit generalizability; not a general-purpose robust-RAG method.
notes: Released public data at github.com/ilanazim/RAGHalu_public_data; brand data proprietary.

title: RAG-QA Arena: Evaluating Domain Robustness for Long-form Retrieval Augmented Question Answering
supports_claims: Long-form RAG-QA evaluation requires coherent multi-document reference answers and pairwise LLM-judge protocols that align with human judgment
Cross-domain robustness of RAG-QA systems can be benchmarked via LFRQA across seven domains, revealing that top LLMs only win 41.3% against human-annotated references
rationale: The paper introduces LFRQA, a multi-domain human-annotated long-form RAG-QA dataset, and RAG-QA Arena, a pairwise LLM-judge evaluation framework that handles conflicting information from multiple documents. It directly contributes to evaluation protocols for robust RAG under unreliable evidence by addressing domain shift, multi-document aggregation, and answer coherence under conflicts. Placement in main:evaluation is appropriate because it is a venue-published benchmark with code/data that a robust RAG survey would cite for evaluation methodology and cross-domain robustness measurement.
caveat: Focuses on text-only QA evaluation; reliability framing centers on cross-domain generalization and reference quality rather than adversarial or poisoned evidence.
notes: EMNLP 2024 main conference; artifacts at github.com/awslabs/rag-qa-arena.

title: LaRA: Benchmarking Retrieval-Augmented Generation and Long-Context LLMs – No Silver Bullet for LC or RAG Routing
supports_claims: Benchmarks comparing RAG vs long-context LLMs reveal that the optimal choice depends on model strength, context length, task type, and retrieval characteristics, with no universal winner.
RAG provides robustness advantages for hallucination detection and mitigates the lost-in-the-middle phenomenon compared to feeding full long contexts.
Prior RAG-vs-LC benchmarks suffer from insufficient context length, data leakage, truncation issues, and unreliable automated metrics, motivating more rigorous evaluation protocols.
rationale: LaRA is an ICML 2025 benchmark with 2326 cases across four QA tasks (location, reasoning, comparison, hallucination detection) and three long-context types, designed to rigorously compare RAG and long-context LLMs across 11 models. It directly informs survey discussions on evaluation protocols for robust RAG and on action-control style routing decisions between RAG and LC under varying conditions. The hallucination detection task and lost-in-the-middle analysis make it directly relevant to robustness under unreliable evidence. Main:evaluation placement is appropriate given its benchmark contribution and methodological critique of prior evaluation pipelines.
caveat: Scope is limited to English QA over long documents and uses GPT-4o as judge, so generalization to multilingual, open-ended, or adversarial evidence settings is not directly established.
notes: PMLR v267 ICML 2025 paper; code and data available at github.com/Alibaba-NLP/LaRA.

title: The Fragile Truth of Saliency: Improving LLM Input Attribution via Attention Bias Optimization
supports_claims: Input saliency methods systematically misattribute importance to irrelevant tokens in long-context prompts, motivating interpretability tools for LLM context use.
Attention bias optimization can causally identify influential input tokens, with applications to behavior steering and reasoning correction.
rationale: This paper focuses on input saliency/attribution methods for LLMs, using a needle-in-a-haystack stress test and proposing Attention Bias Optimization (ABO) for more faithful token attribution. While it touches on long-context use and could be tangentially relevant to understanding how LLMs latch onto distractor versus causal tokens, it does not address retrieval-augmented generation, evidence reliability, knowledge conflict, or any RAG-specific failure mode. The scenario hit on 'biomed/legal/finance' appears spurious (only GSM8K math is used as an applied case). It is too far from the survey's core scope to justify citation.
caveat: Could be cited only as distant background on attribution/interpretability in long-context inputs; risk of overclaiming a connection to RAG evidence robustness that the paper does not establish.
notes: Scenario tag 'domain_biomed_legal_finance' appears mis-assigned; paper is about LLM saliency methods, not domain-specific RAG.

title: Retrieval Augmented Generation or Long-Context LLMs? A Comprehensive Study and Hybrid Approach
supports_claims: Self-reflection routing between RAG and long-context LLMs can reduce cost while maintaining accuracy comparable to full long-context processing.
RAG failures cluster around multi-step reasoning, general or complex queries, and implicit questions requiring holistic context understanding.
Comprehensive benchmarking shows long-context LLMs often outperform RAG but at substantially higher token cost, motivating adaptive evidence-use strategies.
rationale: The paper benchmarks RAG vs long-context LLMs across nine datasets and proposes Self-Route, which uses LLM self-reflection to decide whether retrieved chunks suffice or whether to fall back to full long-context processing. This is directly relevant to action control / adaptive retrieval under potentially insufficient evidence and provides a useful failure taxonomy for RAG (multi-step, general, complex, implicit queries). Placement in main:control is appropriate because the routing mechanism exemplifies a self-reflective abstention/escalation strategy central to robust RAG.
caveat: Self-reflection routing assumes LLM is well-calibrated about answerability; the paper notes performance drops for Gemini and acknowledges dataset leakage and synthetic-data artifact issues that limit generality.
notes: EMNLP 2024 Industry Track; code link is only to needle-in-haystack repo, no Self-Route artifact released.

title: From RAG to Memory: Non-Parametric Continual Learning for Large Language Models
supports_claims: Graph-augmented RAG with Personalized PageRank and LLM-based triple filtering improves robustness across factual, sense-making, and multi-hop associative retrieval tasks.
Recognition-memory style triple filtering can reduce noise from retrieved structured evidence and balance phrase-level versus passage-level signals in KG-based retrieval.
Non-parametric continual learning frameworks built on graph indexing remain stable as the corpus grows, but multi-hop performance degrades faster than single-hop performance.
rationale: HippoRAG 2 is a venue-published (ICML 2025) framework that integrates KG construction, dense-sparse passage integration, and an LLM-based triple filter (recognition memory) to improve retrieval quality and reduce irrelevant evidence in multi-hop and continual-learning RAG settings. It directly contributes to evidence construction and noise filtering, which are core themes for robust RAG under unreliable evidence, and it fits the agent/memory scenario for the survey. Placement in main:modality is appropriate because it serves as a backbone example of memory-oriented RAG; an overclaim risk is treating it as a security/poisoning defense, which it does not address.
caveat: The paper does not target adversarial poisoning or prompt injection; its 'unreliable evidence' handling is limited to LLM-based relevance filtering and graph weighting rather than malicious or conflicting evidence.
notes: ICML 2025 PMLR v267; code at github.com/OSU-NLP-Group/HippoRAG.

title: $LONG^2RAG$: Evaluating Long-Context \& Long-Form Retrieval-Augmented Generation with Key Point Recall
supports_claims: Evaluating long-context, long-form RAG requires recall-oriented metrics that measure how well generated responses incorporate key points from multiple noisy retrieved documents.
Standard truncation in RAG pipelines causes information loss, suggesting long-context handling is important for exploiting retrieved evidence.
rationale: The paper introduces the LONG2RAG benchmark (280 questions, 10 domains, 8 categories, 5 retrieved docs averaging 2,444 words each) and the Key Point Recall (KPR) metric to evaluate how effectively LLMs exploit retrieved long documents in long-form generation. It is directly relevant as an evaluation contribution for the long-context document RAG scenario in the survey, complementing faithfulness/precision-oriented metrics with a recall perspective. Placement in the evaluation/long-context section is appropriate; risk of overclaim is moderate since the benchmark is small (280 questions) and English-only, and it does not directly target adversarial or unreliable evidence.
caveat: Small English-only dataset focused on exploitation of retrieved info rather than reliability under adversarial or contradictory evidence.
notes: Dataset available at GitHub (QZH-777/longrag) per abstract.

title: ChatQA 2: Bridging the Gap to Proprietary LLMs in Long Context and RAG Capabilities
supports_claims: Long-context RAG benefits from long-context retrievers that reduce chunk fragmentation, with accuracy improving as the number of retrieved tokens grows.
Empirical comparisons between direct long-context and RAG show RAG can match or surpass strong long-context LLMs when sufficient top-k chunks are provided.
rationale: The paper presents ChatQA 2, a 128K-context Llama3 model with three-stage instruction tuning and systematic comparisons between RAG and long-context solutions across 4K, 32K, and >100K benchmarks. It contributes useful empirical insights for the long_context_doc scenario, including chunk size/top-k ablations and the role of long-context retrievers in mitigating context fragmentation. It is appropriate as a case study under modality/scenario coverage rather than as core robustness work, since it does not directly study unreliable evidence, noise, or adversarial conditions.
caveat: Focus is on capability extension and accuracy comparison, not on robustness under noisy, conflicting, or adversarial evidence.
notes: ICLR 2025 venue-linked; open-source artifacts on chatqa2-project.github.io.

title: LongRAG: A Dual-Perspective Retrieval-Augmented Generation Paradigm for Long-Context Question Answering
supports_claims: Dual-perspective RAG with a global information extractor and CoT-guided filter improves evidence quality and reduces noise for long-context multi-hop QA.
Mapping retrieved chunks back to source paragraphs preserves contextual structure and mitigates the lost-in-the-middle problem in long-context RAG.
rationale: LongRAG proposes a plug-and-play RAG paradigm combining a hybrid retriever, an LLM-augmented information extractor, and a CoT-guided filter that explicitly targets noise filtering and incomplete-evidence problems in long-context multi-hop QA. It directly addresses unreliable evidence symptoms (lost-in-the-middle, low evidence density, chunk truncation) and provides ablations isolating the contributions of extractor versus filter, which is relevant to a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence. Placement under main:evidence fits because its primary contributions are about evidence construction and filtering rather than calibration or attack defense.
caveat: Evaluation is restricted to three multi-hop QA datasets from LongBench and to one-time retrieval; robustness to adversarial or poisoned evidence is not directly studied.
notes: EMNLP 2024 main proceedings; code and data publicly available.

title: DSLR: Document Refinement with Sentence-Level Re-ranking and Reconstruction to Enhance Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Sentence-level decomposition, re-ranking, and reconstruction can filter irrelevant content within retrieved passages without additional training, improving RAG accuracy.
Preserving original sentence order after filtering matters more than ordering by relevance score, indicating contextual coherence is important for grounding.
rationale: DSLR is an unsupervised refinement framework that decomposes retrieved passages into sentences, removes sentences below a relevance threshold using off-the-shelf rankers, and reconstructs them in original order. It directly tackles the unreliable-evidence problem by filtering irrelevant sentences within fixed-size retrieved passages and shows gains on six open-domain QA datasets including domain-specific and ever-evolving ones. It fits the evidence construction track of the survey as a representative unsupervised, training-free context refinement approach, suitable for appendix coverage alongside RECOMP and similar refiners.
caveat: Workshop paper with limited novelty beyond standard re-rank-and-filter; relies on threshold tuning and inherits errors from the initial BM25 retrieval.
notes: ACL 2024 KnowledgeNLP workshop paper; no explicit DSLR code repo surfaced in text, only BEIR/Pyserini dependencies.

title: RAPID: Long-Context Inference with Retrieval-Augmented Speculative Decoding
supports_claims: RAG drafters can effectively complement long-context LLMs through speculative decoding, integrating retrieval-based and full-context generation paradigms.
Retrieval-augmented inference can maintain robustness to retrieval quality through controlled knowledge transfer parameters, particularly when stronger drafters are used.
rationale: The paper introduces RAPID, which uses RAG as a drafter in speculative decoding to accelerate long-context inference while integrating RAG's selective retrieval benefits with full-context verification. While the primary contribution is efficiency for long-context inference, Section 4.5 demonstrates robustness to retrieval quality (including unrelated retrieval contexts), which is directly relevant to robust RAG under unreliable evidence. The work bridges RAG and long-context paradigms, making it useful as appendix-level support for discussions on combining retrieval with long-context verification.
caveat: The paper's main focus is decoding efficiency rather than robustness to unreliable evidence; the robustness analysis is a secondary contribution and does not deeply explore adversarial or noisy evidence scenarios.
notes: ICML 2025 paper with code available; robustness to retrieval quality discussion is the most relevant aspect for the survey.

title: Retrieval-Augmented Perception: High-resolution Image Perception Meets Visual RAG
supports_claims: Visual RAG can mitigate high-resolution image perception challenges in MLLMs by retrieving query-relevant image crops while preserving spatial layout.
Adaptive retrieval control using model confidence and retrieval scores (RE-Search) can dynamically determine the number of evidence units needed per task type.
Preserving relative spatial relationships among retrieved evidence is critical for cross-instance perception tasks, illustrating evidence-construction principles for multimodal RAG.
rationale: The paper introduces RAP, a training-free visual RAG framework that retrieves image crops, uses a Spatial-Awareness Layout to preserve positional relationships, and applies an A*-style RE-Search guided by model confidence to adaptively choose how many crops to retain. This directly contributes to a robust-RAG survey's multimodal/scenario chapter by showing how evidence construction and confidence-based adaptive retrieval interact in vision settings. Published at ICML 2025 with code available, making it a solid main citation for visual RAG and adaptive evidence selection.
caveat: Focus is on HR image perception accuracy rather than adversarial/noisy evidence robustness; the 'unreliable evidence' framing is implicit (irrelevant crops) rather than explicitly addressing poisoning or conflicting evidence.
notes: Strong candidate for the multimodal/vision RAG section; also useful as a case study for confidence-driven adaptive retrieval in vision.

title: RAG4GFM: Bridging Knowledge Gaps in Graph Foundation Models through Graph Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Graph RAG with multi-level indexing and task-aware retrieval can ground GFM predictions in retrieved subgraph evidence to improve reasoning faithfulness.
Threshold-based relevance filtering during attention fusion and topology enhancement helps suppress low-quality retrieved subgraphs in graph RAG pipelines.
rationale: RAG4GFM is a NeurIPS 2025 graph RAG framework that augments Graph Foundation Models with hierarchical HNSW-based indexing, task-aware retrieval over node/edge/graph spaces, and a fusion module with relevance-thresholded feature and adjacency aggregation. It is relevant to the survey as a representative graph/KG modality case where retrieval grounding aims to reduce hallucinations and where thresholding filters low-quality evidence, but it does not directly study adversarial or unreliable evidence settings. Appendix or modality-section placement is appropriate as a graph scenario exemplar; main claims about robustness under unreliable evidence would overreach.
caveat: Faithfulness/hallucination claims are indirect; the paper does not benchmark against noisy, conflicting, or poisoned retrieval, so it should not be cited as direct evidence of robustness to unreliable evidence.
notes: Code at https://github.com/Matrixmax/RAG4GFM; useful as a graph-RAG scenario citation.

title: Reliable Decision‑Making via Calibration‑Oriented Retrieval‑Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Calibration-aware reranking in RAG can mitigate overconfidence introduced by retrieved evidence and align predicted confidence with downstream decision correctness.
Training a forecasting function with temperature-conditioned soft labels enables adaptive document selection and optional query reformulation when retrieved evidence is insufficient.
rationale: The paper proposes CalibRAG, which trains a forecasting function to predict whether a user decision based on a retrieved document will be correct, then reranks documents by this calibrated confidence and optionally reformulates the query when confidence is below threshold. This directly addresses robust RAG under unreliable evidence by tackling overconfidence on irrelevant or low-utility retrieved documents and by introducing adaptive retrieval/abstention-like behavior. It fits main:control as a calibration and adaptive-retrieval lineage paper, with empirical comparisons against uncertainty calibration, reranking, and SelfRAG baselines across general and medical QA. Overclaim risk is moderate since improvements depend on synthetic supervision from a surrogate user model.
caveat: Calibration labels are derived from a GPT-4o-mini-judged surrogate user model rather than real human decisions, which may bias the forecasting function.
notes: NeurIPS 2025 paper; scenario tag long_context_doc in metadata is loose since experiments are standard QA plus medical QA.

title: Influence Guided Context Selection for Effective Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Inference-time data valuation can quantify per-context contribution to RAG generation quality, integrating query relevance, list-level uniqueness, and generator alignment for noise filtering.
Learned surrogate models can approximate oracle context-influence scores to enable label-free, low-latency context selection that improves robustness to noisy retrieval.
rationale: The paper proposes Contextual Influence (CI) value and a hierarchical surrogate model (CSM) for selecting high-quality contexts in RAG, explicitly targeting irrelevant and noisy retrieved evidence across 8 knowledge-intensive NLP tasks with Llama3 and Qwen2.5. It directly supports the evidence-construction line of a robust RAG survey by reframing context selection as inference-time data valuation and offering a configuration-free positive-CI selection rule. Placement in main:evidence is appropriate because it provides a concrete mechanism for shielding generators from unreliable evidence. Caveat: experiments are text-only on standard QA/fact-checking benchmarks, not multimodal despite the collection tag.
caveat: Despite being tagged vision_multimodal, the paper is text-only on standard NLP benchmarks and requires task-specific CSM training, limiting cross-task generalization claims.
notes: Scenario metadata mismatch: paper is not multimodal; it addresses noise-robust context selection for text RAG.

title: Lift Yourself Up: Retrieval-augmented Text Generation with Self-Memory
supports_claims: Self-generated outputs can serve as an unbounded memory pool that augments retrieval-based evidence beyond a fixed corpus.
Iterative generator-selector loops can refine the quality of retrieved/constructed evidence used for downstream generation.
rationale: The paper introduces Selfmem, which iteratively uses a retrieval-augmented generator's own outputs as memory and a memory selector to pick the best candidate, addressing the bounded-corpus limitation of retrieval. It is relevant to the evidence-construction perspective of a robust RAG survey because it reframes what counts as usable evidence and how to refine evidence quality over rounds. However, it does not directly tackle noisy, conflicting, or adversarial evidence, faithfulness, or abstention, so it fits better as appendix coverage of evidence-construction lineage rather than a main robustness citation.
caveat: Does not address unreliable, conflicting, or adversarial evidence; gains are framed in terms of n-gram metrics on standard NMT/summarization/dialogue tasks rather than robustness.
notes: Code/data at https://github.com/Hannibal046/SelfMemory; NeurIPS 2023.

title: FaithEval: Can Your Language Model Stay Faithful to Context, Even If "The Moon is Made of Marshmallows"
supports_claims: FaithEval provides a fine-grained benchmark for evaluating LLM faithfulness under unanswerable, inconsistent, and counterfactual contexts that simulate unreliable retrieved evidence in RAG.
Even state-of-the-art LLMs struggle to remain faithful to noisy contexts, and larger models do not necessarily exhibit improved faithfulness.
Task-specific abstention instructions can induce sycophantic degradation on normal contexts, highlighting a tension between robustness and routine performance.
rationale: The paper introduces a 4.9K-sample benchmark explicitly targeting RAG-style unreliable evidence: missing information (unanswerable), conflicting documents (inconsistent), and counterfactual fabrications. It evaluates 18 modern open and proprietary LLMs with a rigorous LLM-judge plus human validation pipeline, providing direct diagnostics on faithfulness hallucination under noisy retrieval. This is a venue-backbone evaluation contribution for a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence and naturally belongs in the evaluation section.
caveat: Contexts are LLM-synthesized rather than from real retrieval pipelines, and the inconsistent context construction uses fabricated counter-evidence which may differ from genuine retrieval noise distributions.

title: Crafting Personalized Agents through Retrieval-Augmented Generation on Editable Memory Graphs
supports_claims: Graph-structured editable memory plus RL-based adaptive selection can replace fixed Top-K retrieval in personalized agent RAG.
Adaptive memory selection via reinforcement learning over a memory graph improves downstream QA, form-filling, and user-service tasks compared to naive and partition-based RAG baselines.
rationale: The paper proposes EMG-RAG, combining a three-layer Editable Memory Graph with RL-trained selection over activated subgraphs to support insertion/deletion/replacement of personal memories for smartphone agents. Its relevance to a robust-RAG survey lies in the adaptive (non-fixed-K) retrieval policy and structured memory editing under dynamic, potentially stale evidence, which touches action_control and graph/agent-memory scenarios. It is best cited in an appendix as a representative agent-memory + KG-style RAG instance, not as a core contribution to unreliable-evidence robustness. Overclaim risk: the paper does not directly study noise, conflicts, poisoning, or calibrated abstention.
caveat: Evaluated on a single proprietary business dataset with GPT-4-generated supervision; no explicit treatment of unreliable/adversarial evidence or knowledge conflicts.
notes: Only third-party tool URLs (FAISS, GPTCache) are released; the EMG-RAG implementation and dataset appear proprietary.

title: Multi-Level Information Retrieval Augmented Generation for Knowledge-based Visual Question Answering
supports_claims: Multi-level retrieval combining entity-level and passage-level evidence can mitigate noisy single-step retrieval in multimodal KB-VQA.
Joint end-to-end training of retrievers and generator with query expansion via retrieved entities improves the relevance of evidence used for answer generation.
rationale: The paper proposes MiRAG, a multi-level RAG approach for knowledge-based VQA that performs cross-modal entity retrieval followed by entity-augmented passage retrieval, jointly trained with the answer generator on ViQuAE. It is relevant to a robust RAG survey because it explicitly addresses the problem of irrelevant/noisy passages from single-step retrieval and shows that entity-grounded query expansion yields more truly relevant evidence. Placement in the multimodal/scenario section is appropriate since the core contribution is a vision-text KB-VQA pipeline, not a general robustness or evaluation mechanism.
caveat: Improvements are demonstrated on a single KB-VQA benchmark (ViQuAE) and focus on pseudo-relevance retrieval; the work does not directly study adversarial or systematically unreliable evidence beyond noisy pseudo-labels.
notes: Code reportedly released at github.com/OA256864/MiRAG.

title: VimoRAG: Video-based Retrieval-augmented 3D Motion Generation for Motion Language Models
supports_claims: Cross-modal RAG pipelines (video-to-3D-motion) suffer from error propagation when retrieved evidence is noisy or semantically misaligned with the query.
Preference-based training (McDPO with a dual-alignment reward) can teach generators to selectively rely on or disregard low-quality retrieved evidence, improving robustness.
rationale: VimoRAG is a NeurIPS 2025 video-based RAG framework for 3D motion generation that explicitly identifies and tackles error propagation from suboptimal retrieved videos via a Motion-centric Dual-alignment DPO trainer that teaches the LLM when and how much to rely on retrieved priors. This is a concrete vision-multimodal case study where the model is trained to be robust to unreliable retrieved evidence, and the Mc-R-infinity vs NMc-R-infinity comparison directly evidences improved robustness under random/poor retrieval. It is appropriate as a case study under the multimodal scenario section, but its primary contribution is a motion-generation application rather than general robust RAG theory.
caveat: The robustness contribution is narrow to motion generation and uses a domain-specific dual-alignment reward, so generalization claims to other modalities/tasks should be made carefully.

title: Patent Response System Optimised for Faithfulness: Procedural Knowledge Embodiment with Knowledge Graph and Retrieval Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Combining a domain-specific LLM with a knowledge graph of precedents in a RAG pipeline can reduce hallucination across multiple unfaithfulness error types in legal/patent generation.
Using a consistent backbone LLM as both retriever and generator can improve grounding consistency in domain-specific RAG.
Procedural-knowledge-guided retrieval over a KG plus document context offers a case study of structured RAG in legal/graph_kg scenarios.
rationale: The paper proposes PRO, a patent response system combining a domain-tuned LLM (PRLLM), a patent precedent knowledge graph (PPNet), and multi-path RAG, evaluated with a six-type unfaithfulness error taxonomy adapted from prior work. It is relevant to a robust-RAG survey as a domain-specific KG+RAG case study addressing faithfulness in legal text generation, but its contributions are application-focused rather than offering new mechanisms for handling noisy or adversarial evidence. Appendix placement is appropriate to support coverage of graph_kg and domain-specific RAG scenarios without overclaiming general robustness contributions.
caveat: Domain-bound to patent OA responses with proprietary data; faithfulness gains are reported via human evaluation specific to patent error types and may not generalize to broader unreliable-evidence settings.
notes: Workshop paper (KnowLLM 2024); no public code/data links found in extracted text.

title: Optimizing LLM Based Retrieval Augmented Generation Pipelines in the Financial Domain
supports_claims: RAG systems exhibit pseudo-helpfulness when relevant gold documents are missing from retrieved context, generating loosely related content or hallucinations rather than abstaining.
LLM answer quality in RAG is sensitive to retrieval noise, number of retrieved documents, and gold document position, with even GPT-4 degrading when distractors increase.
Domain-specific (financial) empirical benchmarking reveals robustness gaps between proprietary and open-source LLMs in instruction following and prompt sensitivity.
rationale: The paper systematically benchmarks 6 LLMs across 15 retrieval conditions and 9 prompts on two banking datasets, isolating the effects of gold-document presence, document count, and ordering on generation quality. It directly characterizes failure modes under unreliable evidence (pseudo-helpfulness, distractor sensitivity, position bias) which are central to the survey's scope. Appendix placement is appropriate because the contribution is largely an empirical case study in finance rather than a new method, and the datasets are not released.
caveat: Findings are based on confidential internal banking datasets that cannot be released, limiting reproducibility and external validity beyond the financial domain.
notes: NAACL 2024 Industry Track; useful as a domain case study evidencing pseudo-helpfulness and retrieval-noise sensitivity.

title: Self-RAG: Learning to Retrieve, Generate, and Critique through Self-Reflection
supports_claims: Self-reflective reflection tokens enable adaptive on-demand retrieval and self-critique over retrieved passages, improving robustness to irrelevant or unsupported evidence.
Fine-grained critique tokens (IsRel, IsSup, IsUse) provide a controllable mechanism to enforce evidence grounding and citation faithfulness at inference time.
Segment-level beam search guided by reflection token probabilities allows test-time customization of trade-offs between citation precision and fluency.
rationale: Self-RAG trains an LM to emit special reflection tokens that decide when to retrieve, judge passage relevance, assess support, and rate utility, enabling adaptive retrieval and self-critique. This directly addresses unreliable evidence by filtering irrelevant passages and grounding generations in supported content, with measurable gains in citation precision/recall. It is a venue-backbone ICLR 2024 paper that any survey on robust RAG should cite under action control and adaptive retrieval, also touching evidence use/faithfulness.
caveat: Critic relies on GPT-4 distilled labels and Llama2 base; reflection token accuracy and adaptive thresholding may not generalize to all domains or modalities.

title: Superposition Prompting: Improving and Accelerating Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Parallel prompt-path processing with Bayesian path pruning can filter distracting or irrelevant retrieved documents while accelerating RAG inference.
Structured prompting topologies offer a training-free mechanism to mitigate the LLM distraction phenomenon caused by noisy long-context retrieval.
rationale: The paper introduces superposition prompting, a fork-join DAG prompt structure with Bayesian path pruning that processes retrieved documents in parallel and discards irrelevant ones, improving both efficiency and accuracy on NaturalQuestions-Open and MuSiQue. Its relevance to robust RAG under unreliable evidence comes from the pruning mechanism that filters distracting/irrelevant documents, addressing the noise sensitivity issue. However, the main emphasis is on inference acceleration rather than evidence reliability, so it is best suited as appendix support for context-filtering or long-context robustness discussions.
caveat: Primary motivation is compute efficiency rather than robustness to unreliable evidence; pruning is tested only on standard QA datasets without adversarial or conflicting evidence settings.
notes: ICML 2024 paper with Apple open-source implementation.

title: SV-RAG: LoRA-Contextualizing Adaptation of  MLLMs for Long Document Understanding
supports_claims: Multimodal RAG can scale to long visually-rich documents by using MLLM hidden states as page embeddings and contextualized late interaction for evidence page retrieval.
Dual LoRA adapters over a shared MLLM backbone enable parameter-efficient separation of retrieval and answer generation for multi-page document QA.
rationale: SV-RAG is an ICLR 2025 paper proposing a self-visual RAG framework that uses an MLLM as both retriever (via Col-style late interaction over hidden states) and QA module through dual LoRA adapters, targeting multi-page visually-rich document understanding. It is directly relevant to the multimodal/long-document scenario of a robust RAG survey because it addresses filtering irrelevant pages from hundreds of pages and introduces VisR-Bench as an evaluation resource. Placement as a case study under modality/scenario is appropriate since it focuses on scaling and efficiency rather than on noise, conflict, or adversarial reliability. Overclaim risk: it does not explicitly study unreliable, conflicting, or adversarial evidence.
caveat: Does not address evidence reliability, poisoning, knowledge conflict, or calibration; reliability angle must not be overstated.
notes: ICLR 2025 venue-linked; useful for multimodal long-document RAG retrieval design and VisR-Bench reference.

title: Holistic Reasoning with Long-Context LMs: A Benchmark for Database Operations on Massive Textual Data
supports_claims: RAG systems struggle with holistic reasoning tasks that require aggregating information across many documents, while long-context LMs offer a complementary approach with their own degradation patterns.

Information density, position, and query complexity affect long-context model performance more than raw context length, motivating benchmarks that vary these factors when evaluating RAG vs long-context tradeoffs.
rationale: HoloBench is an ICLR 2025 benchmark that systematically varies context length, information density, information position, and query complexity to evaluate long-context LMs on database-style holistic reasoning tasks. It includes a direct RAG vs LCLM comparison showing that retrieval helps smaller models but hurts larger ones under long contexts, which is relevant evidence for a survey discussing when RAG fails under multi-document aggregation. Best placed as an evaluation reference or appendix coverage since its primary focus is long-context LM benchmarking rather than RAG robustness under unreliable evidence per se.
caveat: The paper does not directly study adversarial or unreliable evidence; its RAG analysis is limited to retrieval noise and aggregation failures rather than evidence corruption or conflict.
notes: Useful for evaluation/long-context boundary discussion and for RAG-vs-LCLM tradeoffs.

title: Unified Generative and Discriminative Training for Multi-modal Large Language Models
supports_claims: Unified generative-discriminative training in MLLMs can enable retrieval-augmented generation within a single model, avoiding retriever-generator optimization mismatch.
Choice of multimodal retriever (CLIP, BLIP-2) can degrade downstream generation in MLLMs, highlighting the importance of retriever quality for multimodal RAG.
rationale: The paper proposes Sugar, a structure-induced joint training framework that unifies generative and discriminative capabilities in MLLMs using Dynamic Time Warping kernels, and demonstrates that the resulting model can perform multimodal RAG without an external retriever. For a robust RAG survey, this is relevant as a multimodal RAG boundary case showing how retriever choice (CLIP/BLIP-2) can hurt generation performance and how integrated retrievers may mitigate this. However, robustness to unreliable evidence is not the core focus, so appendix placement under multimodal/extended coverage is appropriate.
caveat: The paper does not directly study noisy, conflicting, or adversarial evidence; RAG is a secondary application of a training-method contribution.
notes: NeurIPS 2024 paper; project repo mentioned but no explicit URL extracted.

title: Vgent: Graph-based Retrieval-Reasoning-Augmented Generation For Long Video Understanding
supports_claims: Graph-based representation of video clips with shared-entity edges can preserve temporal/semantic dependencies and improve retrieval over chunk-based RAG for long video.
Post-retrieval structured query refinement and aggregation can filter hard-negative retrieved clips and reduce noise-induced reasoning errors in multimodal RAG.
Empirical evidence that ~40-44% of failures stem from correct clips being retrieved yet ignored due to distraction by irrelevant retrievals motivates explicit noise-filtering modules.
rationale: Vgent is a NeurIPS 2025 multimodal RAG method that constructs an entity-linked graph over video clips and adds a structured verification/aggregation step to discard hard-negative retrievals, directly addressing unreliable evidence in long-video RAG. It fits the survey as a representative vision/multimodal scenario with both evidence-construction (graph retrieval) and noise-filtering/control aspects, suitable for case-study treatment in the modality section. The failure-mode analysis (retrieved-yet-wrong) is a useful diagnostic supporting the broader claim that retrieval success is insufficient without post-retrieval reasoning.
caveat: Improvements are reported only on three video QA benchmarks with multiple-choice setups; the noise-robustness claim is indirect (no adversarial or poisoned-evidence evaluation) and relies on a single base-model family.
notes: Project page https://xiaoqian-shen.github.io/Vgent; code availability indicated but data not explicitly released.

title: ParamMute: Suppressing Knowledge-Critical FFNs for Faithful Retrieval-Augmented Generation
supports_claims: Mid-to-deep FFN layers are mechanistically implicated in unfaithful RAG generation, and selectively suppressing their activation can reduce reliance on parametric memory and improve contextual faithfulness.
A consistency-filtered benchmark (CoFaithfulQA) combined with knowledge-preference optimization enables evaluation and mitigation of knowledge-conflict failures in RAG.
rationale: The paper identifies Unfaithfulness-Associated FFNs via correlation and causal NLL interventions, then proposes a suppression-plus-adaptation framework (ParamMute) that calibrates models toward retrieved evidence over parametric memory. It also releases CoFaithfulQA and evaluates on ConFiQA/FaithEval, making it directly relevant to the model_evidence_use chapter of a robust RAG survey on unreliable evidence and knowledge conflict. Placement in main:model is appropriate because it offers both a mechanistic explanation and a method lineage for faithfulness control.
caveat: Experiments focus on QA-style text RAG with a single backbone family for analysis; generalization to multimodal or agentic RAG settings is not directly demonstrated.
notes: NeurIPS 2025 venue confirmed; code at OpenBMB/ParamMute.

title: RealRAG: Retrieval-augmented Realistic Image Generation via Self-reflective Contrastive Learning
supports_claims: Retrieval similarity is not sufficient for useful evidence selection in multimodal RAG; reflective negative mining can select complementary evidence that fills generator knowledge gaps.
Real-object retrieval-augmented image generation can mitigate hallucinations and distortions for fine-grained and unseen objects across diffusion and autoregressive backbones.
rationale: The paper proposes RealRAG, a vision-side RAG framework that trains a reflective retriever via self-reflective contrastive learning to retrieve images carrying knowledge the generator lacks, rather than the most similar ones. This is relevant to a robust RAG survey as a multimodal case where naive similarity-based retrieval yields unreliable or redundant evidence, motivating evidence-construction strategies tailored to generator weaknesses. Placement in the multimodal/scenario section is appropriate; overclaim risk is moderate because the work targets image generation rather than QA-style grounding or knowledge conflict resolution.
caveat: Focuses on image generation realism rather than factual grounding or unreliable evidence in QA; robustness framing is implicit, not under adversarial or noisy retrieval settings.
notes: ICML 2025 paper; project page provided but code/data availability not explicit in excerpt.

title: ChatQA: Surpassing GPT-4 on Conversational QA and RAG
supports_claims: Conversational RAG benchmarks like ChatRAG Bench enable evaluation of grounding, table reasoning, and unanswerable handling across diverse document types.
Incorporating a small amount of unanswerable training samples significantly improves a RAG model's ability to abstain rather than hallucinate when evidence is insufficient.
Fine-tuning single-turn retrievers on conversational query-context pairs can match LLM-based query rewriters for multi-turn retrieval without extra inference cost.
rationale: ChatQA introduces a two-stage instruction tuning recipe, a conversational retriever, and ChatRAG Bench (10 datasets including unanswerable cases and tabular reasoning). For a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence, the most relevant contributions are the unanswerable-case study (showing small amounts of refusal data substantially boost abstention) and the benchmark which explicitly tests context-insufficient scenarios. The conversational retrieval fine-tuning is also a useful evidence-construction reference. Placement as case_study under evaluation is appropriate since the paper's primary thrust is competitive conversational QA quality rather than systematic robustness analysis.
caveat: The paper's main goal is matching GPT-4 on conversational QA rather than systematically studying unreliable evidence; the unanswerable evaluation is a single component, so it should not be overclaimed as a robustness method.
notes: Open-sourced at chatqa-project.github.io including weights, training data, ChatRAG Bench, and retriever.

title: Long-Context LLMs Meet RAG: Overcoming Challenges for Long Inputs in RAG
supports_claims: Increasing retrieved passage count for long-context LLMs follows an inverted-U pattern due to hard negatives, demonstrating the unreliability of larger retrieval contexts.
Retrieval reordering plus RAG-specific fine-tuning (implicit robustness and explicit relevance reasoning) improves robustness to hard negatives in long-context RAG.
Stronger retrievers can produce harder negatives that more severely mislead the generator, complicating the use of precision/recall as adequacy metrics.
rationale: This ICLR 2025 paper systematically diagnoses how hard negatives degrade long-context RAG performance and proposes a training-free reordering method plus two fine-tuning strategies (implicit robustness and explicit intermediate-reasoning relevance identification). It directly speaks to the survey's themes of unreliable evidence (noisy/hard-negative passages), evidence ordering, and robust generator behavior in a long-context scenario. The main:modality placement fits its long-context RAG focus, and it also offers strong cross-cutting evidence for evidence-construction and model-evidence-use sections.
caveat: Experiments focus on QA-style benchmarks with Wikipedia/PubMed corpora and a limited set of retrievers/LLMs; some claims (e.g., why Gemini-1.5-Pro is more robust) remain speculative.
notes: Repo links in PDF are to third-party training/inference tools (axolotl, vllm), not an explicit code release for the method.

title: Hierarchical Planning for Complex Tasks with Knowledge Graph-RAG and Symbolic Verification
supports_claims: KG-based RAG combined with symbolic verification can correct LLM-generated plans and detect execution failures in agentic settings.
Hierarchical decomposition with retrieval over a dynamic knowledge graph improves plan correctness for long-horizon tasks compared to LLM-only or RAG-only baselines.
rationale: The paper proposes HVR, a neuro-symbolic system that combines KG-RAG with hierarchical planning and a symbolic validator to detect and correct unreliable LLM-generated plans for robotic tasks. It is relevant to robust RAG under unreliable evidence primarily from an action-control and graph/agent scenario perspective, since the symbolic validator functions as a verifier/failure detector that mitigates LLM hallucination during plan execution. Appendix placement is appropriate because the work is application-focused on robotic planning rather than directly studying noisy or adversarial retrieved evidence.
caveat: The paper targets robotic planning in a kitchen simulator (AI2Thor) with a fixed ontology; insights on unreliable evidence are indirect and may not generalize to general-purpose RAG settings.
notes: ICML 2025 (PMLR v267); code at github.com/corneliocristina/HVR.

title: Training Large Language Models for Retrieval-Augmented Question Answering through Backtracking Correction
supports_claims: Training methods that reformulate multi-document RAG as a multi-step decision process with self-correction can improve robustness to noisy retrieved documents.
Backtracking-style stepwise preference optimization reduces reliance on costly chain-of-thought annotations while improving the LLM's ability to assess document relevance.
Chain-supervised tuning and label-supervised tuning each have limitations when handling unreliable retrieved evidence in open-domain QA.
rationale: The paper proposes Backtracking Correction, a stepwise RL training approach that teaches LLMs to sequentially assess retrieved documents and self-correct errors, explicitly targeting noise robustness in RAG. It contrasts Label-Supervised Tuning, Chain-Supervised Tuning, and its method on four open-domain QA benchmarks with a real retriever, showing improved discrimination of relevant vs irrelevant documents. This is directly relevant to a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence as a model-side training method for evidence use, and code/data are released. Placement in main:model is appropriate because the contribution is mechanistic (training scheme), not just an evaluation or benchmark.
caveat: Evaluation is limited to open-domain QA with Wikipedia and Contriever; robustness to adversarial or poisoned evidence and multimodal/long-context settings is not directly tested.
notes: ICLR 2025 paper with GitHub artifact; scenario tag long_context_doc is loose since the focus is multi-document open-domain QA rather than truly long-context.

title: Graph-KV: Breaking Sequence via Injecting Structural Biases into Large Language Models
supports_claims: Structural inductive biases injected via KV-cache attention masking can mitigate positional bias and improve multi-hop reasoning over retrieved evidence in graph-structured RAG.
Sharing positional encodings across parallel-encoded source segments reduces context window consumption and provides robustness to distractor documents in long-context citation-graph QA.
rationale: The paper proposes Graph-KV, a structure-aware attention/KV-cache scheme that organizes retrieved chunks as a graph (source/target) with shared positional encodings, evaluated on seven RAG benchmarks, a new ArXiv-QA citation-graph task, and node classification. It is relevant to robust RAG because it directly tackles positional bias and resilience to distractor documents in long-context multi-hop settings, and offers a graph/long-context modality angle. Best placed in the modality/long-context section of the survey as a representative graph-structured RAG method rather than a core reliability backbone.
caveat: Focus is on attention-mechanism efficiency and positional bias; it does not centrally address noise filtering, faithfulness, or calibration under unreliable evidence.
notes: Useful as graph/long-context RAG case alongside multi-hop robustness discussion.

title: InstructRAG: Instructing Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Self-Synthesized Rationales
supports_claims: Self-synthesized rationales can teach LMs to explicitly denoise noisy retrieved contexts, improving accuracy and verifiability over implicit denoising baselines.
Explicit rationale-based denoising remains robust as the number of retrieved documents (and noise ratio) grows, outperforming vanilla SFT and Self-RAG style baselines.
Instruction-following LMs can synthesize generalizable denoising supervision without GPT-4 or human annotation, transferring across QA tasks and even to code generation.
rationale: InstructRAG introduces a self-synthesized rationale framework where an instruction-tuned LM explains how the ground-truth answer is derived from potentially noisy retrieved documents, then uses these rationales for ICL or SFT. It directly targets the unreliable-evidence problem central to the survey, providing both a method and analysis (noise robustness curves, OOD transfer, attention visualization) that fit the model-evidence-use perspective. As an ICLR 2025 paper with released code and consistent gains across five knowledge-intensive benchmarks, it serves as a venue-backbone citation for the section on explicit denoising and faithful use of noisy contexts.
caveat: Despite the scenario tag, the paper is text-only QA and not truly multimodal; claims about general robustness rest on pattern-matching metrics and a single retriever per dataset.
notes: Scenario hit of vision_multimodal appears to be a metadata artifact; the actual contribution is in textual long-context QA RAG.

title: Memory Decoder: A Pretrained, Plug-and-Play Memory for Large Language Models
supports_claims: Parametric memory components can imitate kNN retrieval distributions, offering an alternative to retrieval-augmented inference for domain adaptation.
Plug-and-play memory modules trained via KL alignment with kNN-LM distributions reduce inference overhead compared to retrieval-augmented baselines.
rationale: The paper proposes a small pretrained transformer decoder that imitates kNN-LM retrieval distributions and interpolates with a frozen LLM, evaluated on perplexity and downstream tasks across biomedicine, finance, and law. It is adjacent to RAG (replacing rather than improving retrieval) and does not address unreliable evidence, noisy retrieval, knowledge conflict, attribution, calibration, or adversarial robustness. It is best cited as background on retrieval/memory alternatives in the kNN-LM lineage rather than as core evidence for a robust-RAG survey.
caveat: Risk of overclaiming robustness relevance: the work targets efficiency and domain adaptation, not robustness to unreliable or adversarial retrieved evidence.
notes: NeurIPS 2025 paper with public code at github.com/LUMIA-Group/MemoryDecoder.

title: Chain of Agents: Large Language Models Collaborating on Long-Context Tasks
supports_claims: Multi-agent chain communication can mitigate RAG failures when retrieval misses gold evidence, by enabling full receptive-field coverage over long inputs.
RAG performance depends strongly on re-ranking quality and degrades when the gold answer is not retrieved into the top chunks, motivating robust alternatives for long-context tasks.
rationale: The paper proposes Chain-of-Agents as an alternative to RAG and long-context LLMs for long-input tasks, explicitly diagnosing RAG failure modes (incomplete retrieval, lost-in-the-middle) and showing CoA improves over RAG when retrieval fails. For a survey on robust RAG under unreliable evidence, it is useful as a boundary/comparative method in the long-context/agent scenario rather than a core RAG robustness technique. Appendix citation is appropriate because it competes with RAG rather than improving evidence selection or grounding within RAG.
caveat: CoA is not itself a RAG robustness method; it bypasses retrieval via multi-agent reading, so overclaiming it as a robust-RAG technique would be inaccurate.
notes: Useful for discussing RAG limitations and long-context agent baselines; pairs well with discussions of retrieval sufficiency and lost-in-the-middle.

title: Measuring and Enhancing Trustworthiness of LLMs in RAG through Grounded Attributions and Learning to Refuse
supports_claims: Alignment-based learning-to-refuse improves RAG robustness when retrieved evidence is insufficient by reducing over-responsiveness and hallucinated grounding.
Holistic trustworthiness metrics combining grounded refusal, answer calibration, and citation precision/recall isolate LLM behavior from retriever quality and expose parametric-knowledge leakage.
rationale: The paper introduces TRUST-SCORE (a metric covering grounded refusal, answer correctness calibrated to retrieved docs, and citation groundedness) and TRUST-ALIGN (a DPO-based alignment over 19K paired samples targeting five hallucination types). It directly tackles robust RAG under unreliable evidence by training models to refuse when documents are insufficient and to ground citations, evaluated across LLaMA/Qwen/Phi families on ASQA/QAMPARI/ELI5/ExpertQA. Placement in main:control fits because the central mechanistic claim is action control via learn-to-refuse alignment, with strong secondary evaluation contributions.
caveat: Scenario tag in metadata (code_math_symbolic) is misleading; the paper is general factoid/long-form QA rather than code/math, and the answerability label depends on NLI quality.
notes: Could also be cited under main:evaluation for TRUST-SCORE; venue is ICLR 2025 with public code at declare-lab/trust-align.
